articles.title: When Observation Becomes a Business: America's Growing Debate Over AI Surveillance
articles.summary: Contrasts the old understanding of driving in public, where observation by a passerby ended with the encounter, with today's AI and license plate reader systems that can capture, store, and search years of travel history. He profiles how companies such as Flock Safety built a business on that capability and where the company's own claims need scrutiny.
articles.full_text:
When Observation Becomes a Business: 

America’s Growing Debate Over AI Surveillance

For most of American history, driving on a public road carried a simple understanding: anyone nearby could see you. A passing police officer, another driver, or a pedestrian might observe your vehicle for a moment, and then the encounter was over. That temporary observation is fundamentally different from today’s reality, where artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and automated license plate readers can capture, store, organize, and search years of travel history with a few keystrokes.

Companies such as Flock Safety have built a business around this new capability. Flock states that it does not sell individual photographs or personal data in the traditional sense. Instead, it sells subscriptions that allow law enforcement agencies, businesses, neighborhoods, schools, and other customers to access a searchable platform containing images of vehicles, license plates, timestamps, locations, and other identifying characteristics. Legally, there is a distinction between selling a photograph and selling access to a database. From a privacy perspective, however, many Americans see little practical difference. A private company is deriving commercial value from collecting and organizing information about millions of people who never consented to become part of that system.

The concern is not that one camera captured one photograph. The concern is that thousands of cameras working together can reconstruct a person’s movements across cities, counties, and even multiple states. Over time, those records can reveal where someone worships, seeks medical care, attends political events, visits family, conducts business, or spends the night. Individually, each observation may appear insignificant. Collectively, they can create an extraordinarily detailed picture of a person’s life.

This is where constitutional questions begin to emerge. The Fourth Amendment protects Americans against unreasonable searches and seizures. Courts have long recognized that there is generally a reduced expectation of privacy when traveling on public roads because license plates are intended to be visible. However, modern technology has forced courts to consider whether massive collections of individually lawful observations become something entirely different when they are aggregated into searchable databases.

The United States Supreme Court has already acknowledged this principle in related cases. In United States v. Jones (2012), the Court ruled that attaching a GPS tracker to a vehicle constituted a search under the Fourth Amendment. Several justices went further, expressing concern that prolonged electronic monitoring threatens privacy in ways that traditional surveillance never could. In Carpenter v. United States (2018), the Court held that obtaining extensive historical cell-site location records generally requires a warrant because long-term digital tracking reveals what Chief Justice John Roberts described as the “privacies of life.” Although neither case involved automated license plate readers, both decisions have become central to legal arguments challenging mass surveillance networks.

Those challenges are no longer theoretical. In Virginia, the case of Schmidt v. City of Norfolk directly challenges the constitutionality of Flock Safety’s camera network. The plaintiffs argue that recording and storing the movements of every passing vehicle without individualized suspicion amounts to an unreasonable search. While a federal district court ruled in favor of the city, the case is on appeal and is widely viewed as one of the most significant tests of automated license plate reader technology in the United States.

New York is facing similar scrutiny. A class action lawsuit filed against Westchester County challenges a system that accumulated approximately 1.6 billion license plate scans. The plaintiffs argue that creating and maintaining such an extensive historical database of innocent motorists violates constitutional privacy protections, even if each individual image was lawfully captured on a public roadway. The case reflects a broader legal shift away from debating whether a single camera may observe a vehicle and toward examining whether the government or its private contractors should be permitted to build comprehensive records of everyone’s movements.

Civil liberties organizations, including the American Civil Liberties Union, argue that this is the defining privacy issue of the digital age. Their concern is not ordinary policing but persistent, automated surveillance that transforms everyday travel into permanent records. They warn that databases capable of reconstructing years of travel history can chill free speech, religious exercise, political participation, and freedom of association because people may alter their behavior if they believe every movement is being recorded and retained.

Supporters of automated license plate readers respond that these systems have recovered stolen vehicles, located missing children and vulnerable adults, identified suspects in violent crimes, and provided investigators with valuable evidence that might otherwise have been lost. Those successes are real and have been documented by law enforcement agencies across the country. The debate is not whether technology can assist public safety. It is whether sufficient constitutional safeguards exist to prevent a powerful investigative tool from becoming an infrastructure of routine surveillance directed at the general public.

The legal distinction between observation and surveillance is becoming increasingly important. Observation has always been part of public life. Surveillance implies systematic collection, long-term retention, sophisticated analysis, and broad accessibility. When private companies generate revenue by collecting, organizing, and providing access to these records through subscription-based platforms, the conversation extends beyond criminal investigations into questions of commercial exploitation, constitutional limits, and individual liberty.

America now faces a question the Founders could never have imagined: Does the continuous collection, storage, and commercialization of billions of images and location records fundamentally alter the relationship between citizens and those who watch them? The answer will likely shape Fourth Amendment jurisprudence, privacy law, and the acceptable limits of artificial intelligence in public life for decades to come.

articles.title: Torah, Covenant, and Christ
articles.summary: An observation on the two-thousand-year conversation between Torah and the teachings of Jesus: did Jesus fulfill the Torah and inaugurate the New Covenant, or does the Sinai covenant remain defining without alteration? He frames the debate as one of history, language, and identity, not only theology.
articles.full_text:
Torah, Covenant, and Christ

A Two-Thousand-Year Conversation That Still Shapes the World an observation. 

Few discussions in religion generate more passion than the relationship between the Torah and the teachings of Jesus. For nearly two thousand years, Jews and Christians have wrestled with the same central question: Did Jesus fulfill the Torah and inaugurate the New Covenant promised by the prophets, or does the covenant made at Mount Sinai remain the defining covenant without alteration? The debate is not simply about theology. It is about history, language, identity, and how the Hebrew Scriptures should be read.

The historical starting point is clear. The Torah was given by God to the nation of Israel through Moses at Mount Sinai. Scripture repeatedly identifies it as God’s covenant with Israel. Deuteronomy records Moses declaring that the covenant was made with Israel. Psalm 147 celebrates that God revealed His statutes and judgments to Jacob and had not done so for any other nation. Both Judaism and Christianity acknowledge this historical reality. The disagreement begins with what happened after the coming of Jesus.

Jesus Himself was born Jewish, lived as a Jewish man, worshiped in the Temple, taught in synagogues, observed the biblical feasts, and quoted the Torah throughout His ministry. He never claimed the Torah was evil or unnecessary. Instead, He made one of the most debated statements in history: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). The meaning of the word “fulfill” has become one of the defining questions separating Judaism and Christianity.

For Judaism, the Torah remains God’s enduring covenant with Israel. The Hebrew concept of teshuvah, meaning “return,” stands at the center of covenant life. Repentance is not merely feeling sorry for sin. It is returning to God through confession, remorse, correction, and renewed obedience. The prophets consistently called Israel to return to the Lord. Ezekiel declared that if the wicked turned from their sins and kept God’s statutes, they would live. Hosea urged Israel to return to the Lord with words of repentance. Within this framework, repentance precedes restoration.

Jewish theology also distinguishes between teshuvah and kapparah, or atonement. Repentance describes humanity’s return to God. Atonement describes God’s gracious act of cleansing and restoration. Although the Temple sacrifices played an important role in Israel’s worship, Judaism teaches that they were never intended to replace genuine repentance. Psalm 51 captures this truth when David declares that God desires a broken and contrite heart more than ritual sacrifice performed without sincere repentance.

Christians agree that repentance is essential. Jesus opened His public ministry with a call to repent because the kingdom of heaven was at hand. His apostles preached repentance throughout the Book of Acts. The difference lies in how Christians understand the purpose of Jesus’ death. Rather than viewing the cross as replacing repentance, Christianity teaches that repentance and faith work together, with Christ’s sacrifice accomplishing the atonement that believers receive through faith.

The debate becomes even sharper in Jeremiah 31. The prophet first promises that Israel will never cease to be a nation before God as long as the created order endures. Both Jews and Christians see this as a powerful affirmation of God’s enduring commitment to Israel. Yet only a few verses earlier Jeremiah records God’s promise to establish a “new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah.” Judaism generally understands this as a future covenantal renewal with Israel that does not replace the Torah. Christianity believes Jesus inaugurated this New Covenant, pointing to His words at the Last Supper: “This cup is the new covenant in My blood.”

The earliest followers of Jesus did not immediately abandon Jewish life. They continued worshiping in the Temple, observing Jewish customs, and proclaiming Jesus as Israel’s Messiah. The first major controversy emerged only after large numbers of Gentiles embraced the Christian message. The question was whether non-Jews had to become Jews by accepting circumcision and the full Mosaic covenant. Around AD 49, the apostles gathered in Jerusalem to address the issue. Their decision, recorded in Acts 15, concluded that Gentile believers were not required to enter the Sinai covenant in order to follow Christ. This marked a turning point in Christian history.

The destruction of the Second Temple by Rome in AD 70 accelerated the separation between Judaism and Christianity. Without the Temple, Rabbinic Judaism developed around Torah study, synagogue worship, prayer, and teshuvah. Christianity increasingly spread throughout the Gentile world, emphasizing Jesus as the fulfillment of the Law, the Prophets, and the promised Messiah. Over the following centuries, many church leaders distanced Christianity from its Jewish roots. Some eventually embraced replacement theology, the belief that the Church had permanently replaced Israel in God’s covenant plan. Other Christians rejected that conclusion, pointing to Paul’s teaching in Romans 11 that God’s gifts and calling to Israel are irrevocable.

Language also played a significant role in shaping the debate. The Hebrew Scriptures were translated into Greek in the Septuagint centuries before Jesus. Later they were translated into Latin and eventually into English and many other languages. Each translation carried theological assumptions that sometimes altered how key Hebrew concepts were understood. Words such as torah, teshuvah, kapparah, and berit possess rich meanings that are not always fully conveyed by English terms such as law, repentance, atonement, and covenant. As a result, Jews and Christians sometimes use the same English words while understanding them through very different conceptual frameworks.

Today, the conversation remains as active as ever. Judaism continues to affirm that the Torah covenant remains God’s covenant with Israel and that teshuvah is the God-ordained pathway of restoration. Christianity maintains that Jesus fulfilled the Torah and inaugurated the New Covenant promised by Jeremiah while affirming that God’s promises to Israel remain secure. Increasing numbers of scholars from both traditions have sought to recover the Jewish context of the New Testament, producing a richer and more historically informed dialogue than was common in previous centuries.

The enduring question is not whether the Torah belongs to Israel. Scripture answers that clearly. The deeper question is whether the Messiah promised by the Hebrew prophets has already come and established the New Covenant foretold by Jeremiah, or whether Israel and the world still await that fulfillment. For nearly two millennia, that single question has remained one of history’s most profound theological crossroads, shaping civilizations, influencing cultures, and continuing to inspire sincere seekers on both sides of the conversation.

articles.title: The World's Greatest Influencers: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly
articles.summary: Treats influence as the world's most valuable currency, once held by governments, churches, schools, and news organizations and now reachable by anyone with a smartphone, while algorithms quietly shape what billions see and believe. He argues influence is a tool whose value is set by the character, purpose, and truthfulness of whoever wields it.
articles.full_text:
The World’s Greatest Influencers: 

The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly

Influence has become the world’s most valuable currency. In previous generations, influence was largely concentrated in governments, religious institutions, schools, and news organizations. Today, a single individual with a smartphone can reach more people in an hour than many television networks could a generation ago. At the same time, artificial intelligence, recommendation algorithms, and social media platforms quietly shape what billions of people see, believe, purchase, and discuss each day.

Influence itself is neither good nor evil. It is a tool. Its value is determined by the character, purpose, and truthfulness of the one who wields it.

The positive side of influence is evident in those who educate, inspire, heal, and serve. Humanitarian creators have raised millions of dollars for disaster relief, clean water, and medical care. Scientists and educators have expanded public understanding of medicine, technology, and the natural world. Faith leaders continue to provide moral guidance and hope to billions. Parents, teachers, pastors, coaches, mentors, and volunteers remain among the most influential people on earth, even though their impact rarely trends online.

The darker side of influence is equally powerful. Criminal networks recruit through social media. Scammers exploit trust with increasingly sophisticated AI-generated deception. Political operatives, propagandists, and ideological activists compete for attention by appealing to fear, outrage, and division. Some online personalities build enormous audiences by rewarding controversy over truth, creating environments where misinformation spreads faster than careful investigation.

The ugliest form of influence is often the one people never notice. Algorithms decide which headlines appear, which videos autoplay, which advertisements follow users across the internet, and which opinions receive the greatest visibility. Artificial intelligence now assists in writing, searching, creating, and decision-making, making these systems powerful gatekeepers of information. Increasingly, the battle for society is not simply over ideas, but over attention itself.

Today’s most recognized influencers include world political leaders, technology executives, entertainers, athletes, business leaders, and religious figures. Yet history repeatedly demonstrates that lasting influence is rarely measured by wealth, fame, or follower counts. Civilizations are ultimately shaped by ordinary people who faithfully invest in their families, neighborhoods, workplaces, and communities.

From a biblical perspective, influence is measured by fruit rather than popularity. Scripture teaches that a tree is known by its fruit, reminding us that influence should be evaluated by the lives it transforms, the truth it preserves, and the character it produces. In an age where attention is bought and sold, wisdom requires looking beyond who is speaking and examining what their influence ultimately creates.

The world’s greatest influencers are not always the loudest voices. They are the people and systems that consistently shape how humanity thinks, believes, and lives. The responsibility to discern between healthy and harmful influence has never been greater.

articles.title: Spend Money Creating Time With the People You Love
articles.summary: A reflection on how much money goes to not waiting: faster shipping, newer phones, express everything. He proposes the other use of money, creating time with the people you love, because things wear out and love leaves a legacy.
articles.full_text:
A thought I keep coming back to…

We spend much of our lives trading money for time. We pay extra to have something now instead of waiting. A brand-new phone. A newer car. A bigger house. Faster shipping. Express service. Many times, we’re simply paying not to wait.

But there is another way to spend our money.

Spend it creating time with the people you love.

Take your wife out for dinner instead of buying another gadget. Take your husband on a weekend getaway instead of upgrading the television. Take your children to the zoo, the beach, or the park instead of chasing the next thing. Visit your parents while they’re still here. Drive across town just to have coffee with a friend. Buy your grandparents lunch and ask them to tell the stories you’ve never heard. Show up for your brother’s game. Sit beside someone in the hospital. Take a vacation that brings your family closer instead of filling another room with stuff.

Years from now, no one will gather around talking about the phone you owned, the shoes you wore, or how nice your countertops looked.

They’ll remember the road trips where everyone laughed until they cried. The family dinners that lasted for hours. The fishing trip with Dad. The dance in the kitchen with Mom. The bedtime stories. The hugs. The conversations. The ordinary moments that quietly became life’s greatest treasures.

One day, someone you love will be gone.

And in that moment, you won’t be wishing for a newer car or a larger house. You would gladly trade every dollar in your bank account, every possession in your garage, and every luxury you’ve ever owned for just five more minutes with them.

Invest in relationships. Things wear out. Love leaves a legacy.

God bless. 🙏

articles.title: Arranging the Furniture Around the Hole
articles.summary: On the temptation of those who speak of God to appear as though they have already conquered the sins Christ continually delivers them from. He writes that the devil is delighted when a man starts arranging furniture around the hole so no one notices it, and argues the Christian life is lived in the light.
articles.full_text:
There is a peculiar temptation that comes upon those who stand before others to speak of God. It is not merely the temptation to sin, for that belongs to every man. It is the temptation to appear as though one has already conquered the very sins from which Christ continually delivers him.

A congregation can forgive a broken past far more readily than it can forgive a carefully polished present.

The devil is not disappointed when a man falls. He is delighted when the man begins arranging the furniture around the hole so no one notices it. Time passes. The arrangement becomes familiar. Eventually, even the man himself begins to think the furniture is the house.

The Christian life is lived in the light. Not because Christians have little darkness, but because they have found the only Light that can overcome it.

There is another danger, equally subtle.

The observer may become so occupied with another man’s concealment that he forgets to guard his own heart. It is entirely possible to love truth and yet become hardened by it. Truth without charity ceases to resemble Christ. Charity without truth ceases to be charity at all.

If a shepherd has concealed things that ought to have been confessed, the injury is not only to himself. A shepherd teaches as much by what he hides as by what he proclaims. Sheep instinctively learn whether honesty is safe. If they discover that appearances are rewarded while openness is costly, they too will begin wearing masks.

This is why Scripture requires so much of those who lead. The requirement is not perfection. It is reality.

The cross does not require that a man arrive without scars. It requires that he stop pretending they are not there.

A church becomes healthy not when it has leaders with flawless histories, but when it has leaders who no longer fear the truth. Such a house possesses a curious freedom. Confession is not humiliation but liberation. Repentance is not disgrace but the doorway to joy. Grace ceases to be a doctrine and becomes the atmosphere everyone breathes.

The gravest question, therefore, is not whether a pastor has failed. Every pastor has. The question is whether the house is built upon truth strong enough to bear the weight of failure without resorting to disguise.

For a house built upon Christ does not collapse because sinners enter it. It begins to weaken only when sinners conclude that the safest place to hide is behind the pulpit.

Ralph Koschnitzke

articles.title: Following the Money: Why Toledo Keeps Showing Up
articles.topic: Toledo and Ohio: public affairs and history
articles.summary: Prompted by a federal indictment out of Mansfield naming Toledo as an alleged supply city, he asks why northwest Ohio keeps appearing in major federal drug investigations. His answer is position, not character: Toledo sits between Detroit, Cleveland, Chicago, and the Canadian border, and the same routes that move legitimate commerce can be exploited by organized crime.
articles.full_text:
FOLLOWING THE MONEY: 

WHY TOLEDO KEEPS SHOWING UP

The recent federal indictment out of Mansfield caught my attention for one reason: Toledo was named as one of the alleged supply cities.

That raises a bigger question.

Why does northwest Ohio continue to appear in major federal drug investigations?

The answer isn’t that Toledo is uniquely criminal. It’s that Toledo is uniquely positioned.

Sitting between Detroit, Cleveland, Chicago, and the Canadian border, Toledo is a major transportation hub. The same highways, rail lines, and shipping routes that move billions of dollars in legitimate commerce can also be exploited by organized crime.

Federal investigations over the years have revealed similar patterns:

• Multi-city trafficking networks.
• Interstate transportation.
• Cash movement through 
   legitimate businesses.
• Shell companies and financial layering.
• Firearms and narcotics tied 
   to organized distribution.
• Sophisticated money laundering methods.

Notice the pattern. Investigators don’t simply follow drugs anymore. 

They follow the money.

It’s also important to separate fact from assumption.

Just because a car wash, restaurant, convenience store, or used car dealership has appeared in a criminal case does not make those businesses suspicious. Thousands of honest owners operate these businesses every day.

The business isn’t the crime.

The alleged misuse of a business is.

The Mansfield case is still before the courts, and everyone charged is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. But it reminds us that organized crime often hides behind ordinary commerce.

The real story isn’t one car wash.

It’s how criminal organizations exploit geography, transportation networks, and financial systems.

If we want safer communities, we have to understand the patterns—not stereotype the businesses.

Knowledge follows evidence. Evidence follows the money.

articles.title: Toledo's New Reuse Center Opens on Creekside
articles.topic: Toledo and Ohio: public affairs and history
articles.summary: A local write-up on the new Clean Toledo Recycling Center at 3900 Creekside Ave, open year-round for self-service drop-offs with proof of Toledo residency, and on Lucas County's new materials recovery facility. He notes what the center accepts, what it replaces, and closes with practical notes on Toledo's free brick and backyard build scene.
articles.full_text:
# Toledo's New Reuse Center Opens on Creekside

Toledo finally went year-round for drop-offs, which is huge if you've been chasing seasonal Clean Toledo events.

The new Clean Toledo Recycling Center at 3900 Creekside Ave opened June 2nd. It's self-service, 

Tuesday through Saturday 8:30am to 4pm, some city releases list 4:30pm close, and you do need proof of Toledo residency to get in. Think of it as your everyday spot for the usual stuff — recyclables, electronics, scrap metal, appliances without refrigerant, food waste, yard waste, and gently used items in good condition. Grass clippings aren't accepted. It's replacing those big seasonal free refuse drop-offs. 

The other big piece is Lucas County's new materials recovery facility. That's the $30M, 60,000 sq ft plant going in on 15 acres along Kuhlman Drive and South Ave near I-75, built on a former landfill. It's supposed to be operational in 2026 and will process about 30,000 to 35,000 tons of curbside recycling a year so Toledo doesn't have to truck it 90 miles to Oberlin. 

For free bricks, cinder blocks, flagstone and lumber — that stuff won't go through Creekside, but here's where folks are actually finding it this year:

Marketplace is still your best bet in 43609 — set a saved search for "free bricks" "free blocks" "free lumber" "free flagstone" and turn on alerts, the good piles go in under an hour. Same with Craigslist Toledo free section, plus the Buy Nothing Toledo and Freecycle Toledo groups on Facebook.

If you want reclaimed on the cheap instead of free, check Habitat ReStore in Maumee/Toledo — they take and resell bricks, blocks, pavers and unused lumber, and local salvage yards like Resource Reclamation Toledo at 5400 N Detroit Ave and Re-Cre8 at 1001 Brown Ave often have demo brick and dimensional lumber. Greenlight Pallet at 837 Buckingham is great for pallet wood and clean lumber for backyard builds, and Clean Wood Recycling on W Bancroft takes clean wood if you need to dump scraps. 

Pro tip from your backyard build pattern — bring a truck, a dolly, and gloves when you message. Most free brick posts in Toledo are "you haul, first come" from a driveway tear-out in Old West End or Point Place. If you can pick up same-day, you get it.

articles.title: Leadership, Control, and the Missing Conversation
articles.summary: Starts from social media warnings about manipulative people, flatterers, cowards, greedy people, and false friends, and argues the Bible named these patterns long before Machiavelli. His point: the real issue is not simply bad people but unhealthy systems that reward unhealthy behavior.
articles.full_text:
Leadership, Control….

and the Missing Conversation

Social media is full of warnings about manipulative people. One recent post lists flatterers, cowards, greedy people, and false friends. Whether those exact words came from Machiavelli or not, the behaviors are real. History is full of them.

The Bible recognized these patterns long before Machiavelli wrote The Prince. The difference is that Machiavelli often explained how to survive in a world driven by power. Scripture teaches us how to live in a world ruled by truth.

The real issue is not simply bad people. It is unhealthy systems that reward unhealthy behavior.

The Flatterer…

A flatterer tells people what they want to hear to gain influence.

“The mouth of a flatterer works ruin.” Proverbs 26:28

Encouragement builds people. Flattery uses people.

The Fearful Leader….

Fear changes decisions.

A fearful leader may protect a position instead of protecting people. Peter denied Jesus out of fear, but he repented and was restored.

Fear is human. Living by fear is destructive.

The Power Chaser……

Some people are loyal only to influence.
When power shifts, their loyalty shifts.

Jesus taught that greatness is found in serving, not climbing.

The False Friend…

A false friend smiles in public but tears down in private.

David experienced this.

“Even my close friend, someone I trusted… has turned against me.” Psalm 41:9

True friends confront with love instead of gossiping in secret.

The Greedy Heart……

Greed is about far more than money. People can hunger for attention, recognition, titles, influence, or control.

Jesus warned us to guard against every kind of greed because the heart is never satisfied by getting one more thing.

The Missing Conversation……..

Most discussions focus on unhealthy leaders.  The deeper issue is unhealthy systems.

Over time, organizations can slowly reward the very behaviors they once opposed.

Authority begins protecting itself.
Image becomes more important than truth.

Questions become threats. Loyalty shifts from Christ to personalities. Leadership becomes gatekeeping instead of equipping.

Information is controlled instead of shared. Spiritual language begins replacing accountability.

None of these changes usually happen overnight. They happen one small compromise at a time.

The Missing Piece……….

There is another truth we often ignore. Followers help create the leaders they reward.

Israel asked for a king like the surrounding nations. God warned them what would happen, but they wanted visible strength more than faithful leadership.

That pattern has never disappeared…….

Churches that reward charisma over character eventually produce charismatic leaders with weak character. Organizations that reward results over integrity eventually promote people willing to sacrifice integrity.

Communities that value image over truth eventually choose leaders who manage appearances instead of reality. Healthy cultures produce healthier leaders.

Unhealthy cultures eventually reward unhealthy leadership.

The Biblical Pattern

Jesus led differently.

He welcomed honest questions.
He corrected His disciples.
He admitted no deception.
He washed feet instead of demanding status.
He shared authority.

He pointed people to the Father rather than building a following around Himself. The apostles followed the same pattern.

Biblical leadership exists to mature people, not make them dependent.

The goal is not followers who need permission for every decision. The goal is mature believers who know Christ, understand Scripture, listen to the Holy Spirit, and can discern truth for themselves.

A Leadership Checkup…………..

Any leader, church, ministry, business, or organization should be willing to ask these questions like…

Can people ask hard questions without fear?
Is truth valued more than image?

* Does authority serve or protect itself?
* Are leaders accountable?

Is disagreement handled with humility?
Are new leaders being developed?

Is Christ clearly greater than every personality?

Healthy leadership welcomes these questions. Unhealthy leadership fears them.

Why This Matters for Evangelism…..

Many people are not rejecting Jesus. They are rejecting experiences where control replaced service, image replaced truth, and personalities replaced Christ.

The answer is not better branding.

It is visible integrity.

When leaders are humble, accountable, transparent, and willing to repent, the gospel becomes believable because people see the character of Christ instead of the pursuit of power.

The church’s greatest witness is not impressive programs, famous personalities, or polished presentations.

It is ordinary believers and faithful leaders who quietly reflect Jesus. That kind of leadership does more than build healthy churches.

It opens hearts to the gospel.

And that is the true goal of biblical leadership: not building bigger platforms, but making faithful disciples and creating more opportunities for authentic evangelism which I consider the primary action after all the performance stops…. And words stop being echoed…

Ralph Koschnitzke

articles.title: The Lamed-Vavniks: Hidden People Who Sustain the World
articles.summary: Considers the Jewish mystical tradition of the Lamed-Vavniks, hidden humble people whose quiet compassion helps sustain the world. He declines the claim of exactly thirty-six righteous people but affirms the broader pattern: God delights in those who serve in secret and remain faithful in obscurity.
articles.full_text:
The idea of the Lamed-Vavniks comes from Jewish mystical tradition, not Scripture. It speaks of hidden, humble people whose quiet compassion helps sustain the world. Whether or not the tradition itself is true, it points to something recognizable: history is often shaped by ordinary people who faithfully love, serve, pray, and give without seeking recognition.

From my perspective, I don’t embrace the mystical claim that exactly thirty-six righteous people preserve the world. Scripture teaches something broader. God delights in those who serve in secret, remain faithful in obscurity, and reflect Christ without needing applause. Their names may never be widely known, but their lives bear fruit that only God fully sees.

As Ralph Koschnitzke, this post reminded me of a few friends. Not because I believe the legend itself, but because I’ve watched them quietly invest in others without seeking attention or credit. They simply love people, serve faithfully, and keep showing up. Whether anyone notices or not, those are the kinds of lives that leave a lasting mark. While I believe Christ alone is the One who sustains the world, I also believe He often chooses ordinary, humble people to quietly carry His love into it.

RK

articles.title: Ancient Categories, Modern Questions: What the Bible and Jewish Tradition Actually Say
articles.summary: Examines a popular claim that ancient Jewish texts recognized eight genders and that Jesus would therefore have accepted today's understanding of gender diversity. He confirms the Mishnah and Talmud do name categories such as androgynos, tumtum, saris, and aylonit, but argues they are not descriptions of gender identity as the term is used today.
articles.full_text:
Ancient Categories, Modern Questions: What the Bible and Jewish Tradition Actually Say

A popular Facebook post claims that ancient Jewish texts recognized “eight genders,” followed by the conclusion that Jesus, as a first-century Jew, would have accepted today’s understanding of gender diversity. It sounds compelling, but it blends historical facts with modern assumptions in ways that deserve a closer look.

The ancient Jewish writings do contain references to categories beyond simply “male” and “female.” Terms such as androgynos, tumtum, saris, and aylonit appear in the Mishnah and Talmud. These are real categories, but they are not descriptions of gender identity as that term is understood today.

The rabbis were not constructing a spectrum of identities. They were wrestling with difficult legal questions involving people whose biological development was atypical or whose reproductive capacity differed from the norm. Their concerns were practical: Who inherits property? Who can marry? Which commandments apply? How should uncertain biological cases be handled under Jewish law?

The key distinction is that these categories were based on observable physical realities, not on an individual’s internal sense of identity.

This is where today’s discussion often loses clarity.

Modern conversations combine several very different concepts under the word “gender.” Intersex conditions involve biological variations that have existed throughout history. Gender dysphoria describes a psychological experience in which a person’s internal identity does not align with their biological sex. Medical transition involves hormones and surgery. Nonbinary identities reflect contemporary philosophical and cultural understandings of personhood. These are not interchangeable concepts.

The Bible begins with a foundational statement: “Male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). Jesus reaffirmed this creation pattern when He quoted Genesis in Matthew 19:4. That affirmation was not made out of ignorance of biological exceptions. Jesus also acknowledged eunuchs in Matthew 19:12, recognizing that some people are born differently, some are altered by others, and some choose celibacy for the Kingdom.

The existence of exceptional biological conditions does not erase the general pattern of creation. In the same way, acknowledging people born with congenital limb differences does not change the reality that human beings are ordinarily created with two arms and two legs. Exceptions call for compassion and wisdom; they do not redefine the pattern.

Can a biological male become a biological female, or vice versa?

Medicine today can alter appearance, hormone levels, secondary sex characteristics, legal documents, and social presentation. Those changes are significant and deserve to be discussed honestly. At the same time, current medical science cannot change every aspect of biological sex. Chromosomes, reproductive organization, and many developmental characteristics remain tied to one’s biological sex throughout life.

Recognizing that fact is not an argument against treating people with dignity. Every human being bears the image of God and deserves respect, compassion, and truthful conversation. Christians should reject cruelty, ridicule, and dehumanization while also resisting the pressure to redefine reality in ways Scripture and biology do not support.

The Facebook meme contains a historical truth: ancient Jewish literature discusses several categories of people with atypical biological development.

Its conclusion, however, goes beyond the evidence.

The rabbis were not teaching eight modern gender identities. They were creating legal classifications for uncommon biological circumstances while continuing to understand humanity through the creation framework of male and female. Jesus inherited that worldview and affirmed it.

The modern debate is ultimately not about whether ancient Judaism recognized biological complexity. It did. The real question is whether biological complexity should be understood as evidence for an unlimited spectrum of identities or as exceptional cases within an ordered creation.

History answers the first question one way. Scripture answers the second.

The two should not be confused.

articles.title: Love Has the Courage to Correct
articles.summary: Challenges the belief that love and correction stand in opposition: in Scripture, love is often the very reason correction exists. He calls for a church culture where humility welcomes correction, while adding that discernment, wisdom, and maturity decide who should carry a burden for a situation.
articles.full_text:
And… 

Love Has the Courage to Correct

One of the greatest misunderstandings in the Church today is the belief that love and correction stand in opposition to one another. They do not. In Scripture, love is often the very reason correction exists.

God corrects those He loves. A loving parent disciplines a child. A faithful friend speaks the truth even when it is difficult to hear. In the same way, the Church is called to cultivate a culture where humility welcomes correction rather than resists it.

This does not mean every believer is appointed to confront every person or comment on every controversy. Discernment is needed. Wisdom is needed. Maturity is needed. There is a significant difference between carrying a burden for the health of Christ’s body and building an identity around exposing its weaknesses.

Yet neither should we confuse silence with love.

When abuse, manipulation, or harmful teaching is ignored in the name of preserving peace, the result is not unity. It is often the protection of unhealthy systems at the expense of wounded people. Genuine peace is never established by avoiding the truth. It is established when truth and grace meet together in humility.

Jesus modeled this balance perfectly. He welcomed the broken, restored the repentant, and extended extraordinary mercy to those who came to Him in faith. Yet He also confronted hypocrisy without hesitation when it harmed others or distorted the Father’s heart. His strongest words were not reserved for those struggling with sin, but for those who used spiritual influence without integrity.

Correction, when led by the Holy Spirit, is not an act of condemnation. It is an invitation to restoration. Its purpose is never humiliation but healing. It seeks repentance rather than revenge, reconciliation rather than division, and freedom rather than control.

Every believer should desire a heart that remains teachable. None of us has arrived. Every one of us has blind spots that only the grace of God and the loving correction of others can reveal. A mature disciple is not the one who never needs correction. A mature disciple is the one who responds with humility when correction comes.

There are also moments when addressing harmful patterns within the Church becomes necessary for the sake of those who are vulnerable. This should never be driven by anger, personal ambition, or the desire to win arguments. It must always be motivated by love for Christ, love for His people, and a sincere hope that what is broken can be made whole.

The goal has never been to expose people. The goal is to reveal Christ. Sometimes that happens through encouragement. Sometimes it happens through correction. In both cases, love remains the motive.

May we become people who love deeply enough to speak the truth, humble enough to receive the truth, and wise enough to know the difference between protecting a reputation and protecting the people God has entrusted to our care. That kind of love does not weaken the Church. It strengthens it, because it reflects the heart of Christ Himself.

articles.title: The View From the Pew
articles.summary: Argues that bringing theology back into everyday language may be one of the healthiest things happening in the Church. Deep theology is valuable, he writes, but if the average believer cannot understand what is being said, something important has been missed; Jesus spoke into people's lives rather than over their heads.
articles.full_text:
The View From the Pew

Why bringing theology back to everyday language may be one of the healthiest things happening in the Church.

There is something refreshing about conversations that take theology out of the ivory tower and bring it back to the kitchen table.

Not because deep theology isn’t valuable. It is. But if the average believer cannot understand what is being said, we’ve missed something important.

Jesus never spoke over people’s heads to prove His authority. He spoke into their lives to reveal His Father’s heart.

Today, many conversations within the Church are wrapped in language that unintentionally creates distance. Terms like ekklesia, apostolic alignment, covenant relationship, governmental authority, and ecclesiology all have legitimate meaning. Yet they can also create the impression that spiritual understanding belongs primarily to experts.

It doesn’t.

The Kingdom was first announced to fishermen, farmers, tax collectors, widows, laborers, and children.

The gospel was never designed to require a theological dictionary before it could transform a life.

That is why I find myself asking simpler questions.

If a pastor is wrong, can anyone say so?

If someone is being hurt, should the Church remain silent?

Where is the line between gossip and accountability?

Why do some conversations become so complicated that ordinary believers feel disqualified from participating?

Those are not rebellious questions. They are honest ones.

Somewhere along the way, many Christians began placing spiritual leaders into a category all their own. We respect pastors, teachers, apostles, and prophets, as Scripture instructs. But respect is not the same as elevation.

Pastors are people.

Teachers are people.

Prophets are people.

They wrestle with pride, fear, fatigue, misunderstanding, and blind spots just like everyone else. They need grace. They need correction. They need accountability.

So do we.

The apostle Peter called himself a fellow elder. Paul openly admitted his weaknesses. James warned that teachers would be judged more strictly. The closer we read Scripture, the less interested the apostles seemed in creating celebrity and the more interested they were in creating mature disciples.

Perhaps we’ve made some things harder than they need to be.

The average believer doesn’t wake up wondering about ecclesiology. They wake up wondering how to follow Jesus at work, how to forgive someone who hurt them, how to raise faithful children, and how to recognize truth in a confusing world.

Those are the conversations worth having.

Maybe the healthiest thing we can do is remove some of the unnecessary distance between the platform and the pew.

Because at the foot of the cross there are no spiritual celebrities.

Only redeemed people following the same Savior.

The shepherd still smells like sheep.

And that’s exactly how it should be.

RK

articles.title: What Are We All Doing? The Pace of Life
articles.summary: Prompted by a Facebook post and a weekend conversation with Tanya, he reflects on how life since around 2020 has lost its natural rhythm, with everyone running without arriving. He argues progress should make us more human, not less, and points to stronger families, neighbors who know each other, and churches that function as families.
articles.full_text:
I came across a post on Facebook that made me stop and think.

It wasn’t because every point was right. Some of the claims are debatable, and a few deserve careful evidence before they’re accepted. But underneath all of that was a question I think many people quietly wrestle with.

What are we all doing?

Ironically, Tanya and I were discussing this very thing over the weekend. We weren’t talking about one specific news story or political issue. We were talking about the pace of life itself, and how so many people seem to feel like they’re constantly running without ever really arriving.

Since around 2020, there’s been a growing sense that life has lost its natural rhythm.

We’re always chasing the next thing. The next paycheck. The next promotion. The next vacation. The next achievement. Yet somehow we rarely arrive at the place where we’re simply able to enjoy the life we’ve been working so hard to build.

Previous generations weren’t strangers to hardship. The 1970s dealt with inflation and political scandals. The 1980s experienced rapid economic and cultural change. The 1990s had wars, recessions, and uncertainty.

Life wasn’t easier.

It was slower.

There were natural stopping points. Work usually stayed at work. The evening news eventually ended. Stores closed. Families gathered around dinner tables. Kids disappeared outside until dark. Churches, civic groups, neighborhood organizations, and local communities gave people a genuine sense of belonging.

Today, many of those boundaries have disappeared.

Before we’ve even gotten out of bed, we’ve absorbed headlines, opinions, advertisements, messages, and enough information to keep our minds racing all day. Then we’re expected to stay productive, informed, successful, healthy, attractive, organized, and available—all at once.

The biggest change may not be technology itself.

It’s that our attention has become the product.

Every notification, recommendation, breaking headline, and endless scroll is competing for the same limited resource: our focus.

Technology has brought incredible benefits, but every tool raises an important question: Is it serving us, or are we slowly serving it?

I don’t think most people are chasing happiness anymore.

I think they’re chasing the feeling of finally not being behind.

The answer isn’t to romanticize the past. Every generation has had its struggles.

The answer may be to recover what we’ve gradually lost: unhurried conversations, real community, stronger families, neighbors who know each other, churches that function as families rather than events, and time to be fully present with God and one another.

Progress should make us more human, not less.

That’s the part of the Facebook post that stayed with me, because it echoed a conversation Tanya and I had just days earlier.

R. ✌️

articles.title: Be the Example, Not the Salesman
articles.summary: Tells churches built on Christ to be the example rather than salesmen of a religious culture: do not market Christianity while neglecting Christ. He argues Jesus formed a family that walked together every day, not an organization that gathered once a week, and that everything built should look more like Him and less like us.
articles.full_text:
If you’re going to be a church built on Christ, then be the example, not the salesman of a religious culture. Don’t market Christianity while neglecting Christ. Don’t teach people to admire Jesus from a distance while failing to live like Him up close.

Jesus doesn’t need better branding. He doesn’t need to be made relevant, trendy, or culturally acceptable. He is the standard by which every culture, every tradition, every denomination, and every philosophy is measured.

Too often we’ve compartmentalized Him into programs, services, titles, and Sunday mornings. We’ve reduced the Kingdom to an event instead of a way of life. Jesus didn’t establish an organization that gathered once a week. He formed a family that walked together every day.

If we preach love, let people experience it. If we preach discipleship, let someone walk beside them. If we preach grace, let the wounded find safety. If we preach truth, let it be spoken with compassion. Our message loses credibility when our lives don’t reflect it.

The Church was never called to mirror the culture around it or simply preserve the culture behind it. It was called to reflect Christ. The world doesn’t need a better performance. It needs to encounter a people who actually resemble Jesus.

Christ is not an accessory to our ministry. He is the foundation, the pattern, the message, and the mission. If He is truly the Head of the Church, then everything we build should look more like Him and less like us.

RK

articles.title: Toledo's Water Billing System Needs More Than Rules. It Needs Transparency.
articles.topic: Toledo and Ohio: public affairs and history
articles.summary: An open letter about Toledo water billing, built on his own experience moving into a home with its original meter just as the city began replacing older meters. He argues the billing system knows exactly what a resident owes and when, while the process for questioning whether a bill is correct stays hard to understand, and asks for transparency in the meter replacement process.
articles.full_text:
Toledo’s Water Billing System Needs More Than Rules. It Needs Transparency.

Every month, Toledo residents receive water bills with clear due dates, late fees, payment requirements, and collection deadlines. The system knows exactly when a payment is due and exactly what happens if it isn’t made.

When a resident questions whether a bill is correct, the process becomes much harder to understand.

Our experience is one example.

When we moved into our home more than three years ago, the house still had its original water meter. Around that time, the City began notifying residents that older water meters would be replaced with newer technology.

Our experience with the water system actually began on the day we moved in. During the transfer of utility service into our name, the water was shut off, and we spent our first night in the home without running water. The City had to come out during that process.

Later, after receiving an unusually high water bill, we contacted the Water Department because we believed something wasn’t right.

As the meter replacement process began, additional complications were discovered. The water shutoff had to be located, and the existing meter connections required plumbing repairs before the new meter could be installed.

The City technician told us he was not authorized to perform the plumbing work needed to complete the installation. Because of that, we had to hire a plumber to make the necessary repairs before the City could return and replace the meter.

What should have been a straightforward meter replacement became multiple appointments involving the City, a private plumber, and additional scheduling. Those circumstances significantly extended the timeline through no fault of our own.

Despite those circumstances, when our request was ultimately reviewed, the discussion centered on how much time had passed rather than whether the original billing was accurate or whether the delays associated with the meter replacement process should have been considered.

That experience led us to examine Toledo’s utility dispute process.

What we found raises legitimate questions.

The Toledo Municipal Code generally requires a written appeal to be filed within 60 days of the disputed bill. The ordinance also gives the Utilities Administration Commissioner discretion to consider a late appeal when extenuating circumstances prevented a timely filing.

At the same time, the City’s public guidance also refers customers to a 30-day period after initial contact with Customer Service to begin the appeals process.

For the average resident, those timelines are not immediately clear or consistent.

Government has every right to establish procedures.

Government also has a responsibility to make those procedures understandable.

We also found that Toledo has been aggressively addressing more than $60 million in delinquent utility balances. Payment plans, collection activity, and shutoff procedures are clearly communicated. The City understandably places significant emphasis on collecting the revenue needed to operate its utility system.

No reasonable person disputes that responsibility.

What concerns us is balance.

When the City believes a resident owes money, the process moves with urgency.

When a resident believes the City may have made a mistake, that same urgency should exist.

A government should pursue accuracy as diligently as it pursues payment.

During our research, we tried to answer some basic questions.

How many water billing disputes are filed each year?

How many customers receive billing adjustments?

How many appeals are denied?

How many are dismissed because of procedural deadlines?

How long does the average appeal take?

How often does the Utilities Administration Commissioner exercise the authority granted by ordinance to accept a late appeal because of extenuating circumstances?

Those are not obscure questions.

They are measurements of how a public process performs.

We looked for annual reports from the Utility Appeals Board, which City rules require to maintain records of its work and report annually to the Mayor and City Council.

We also searched for publicly available statistics showing how many billing disputes are filed, how many are granted, how many are denied, how many are dismissed because of deadlines, and how long the average appeal takes.

We could not readily locate those reports or performance statistics.

We also found public posts from other residents describing unexpected water usage, questions following meter changes, and billing disputes. Individual experiences do not prove a systemic problem, but they do show that our situation is not unique.

The issue is not whether every customer is right.

The issue is whether the public has enough information to determine whether the system itself is working fairly.

There is also a human cost.

For most families, a utility bill is not just another piece of mail. It is tied to household budgets, rent or mortgage payments, groceries, medications, and the basic necessity of water. When residents cannot get a clear answer to a legitimate question, uncertainty becomes stress. Hours are spent making calls, gathering records, waiting for decisions, coordinating contractors, and worrying about additional fees or possible service interruption.

Government exists to serve the public. A process that is clear, transparent, responsive, and accountable reduces unnecessary stress and strengthens confidence in public institutions. When the process feels confusing or inaccessible, frustration grows, trust erodes, and the relationship between citizens and their government suffers.

Transparency replaces speculation with facts.

Performance data builds public confidence.

If Toledo published annual statistics on billing disputes, appeal outcomes, resolution times, procedural dismissals, and the exercise of discretionary authority for late appeals, residents could evaluate the process using evidence instead of anecdotes.

This is not an accusation of misconduct.

It is a request for accountability and transparency.

We are not asking for special treatment.

We are asking for the same standard every taxpayer should expect.

If government can measure collections, it can measure corrections.

If government expects accountability from its citizens, citizens have every right to expect accountability from government.

If Toledo’s water billing system is working well, publish the numbers.

If improvements are needed, acknowledge them.

Either outcome strengthens public trust.

We invite Toledo residents to share their own experiences, whether positive or negative.

Were your questions answered?

Was the process explained clearly?

How long did it take?

What was the outcome?

Please keep comments factual, respectful, and based on your own experience. The purpose is to gather information, compare experiences with publicly available information, and better understand how the system works in practice.

Comments intended only to troll, insult, derail the discussion, or provoke arguments will be removed and simply noted as part of our research into public discourse. They do not contribute evidence or advance the conversation.

Good government should never fear honest questions.

Good citizens should never fear asking them.

Our individuals and businesses in this historical community are more than just numbers….  

TOLEDO has lived the impact of this very problem for decades… look around you. 

Respectfully,

Tanya Goff and Ralph Koschnitzke

Subject: 

Request for Reconsideration of Water Billing Appeal

Dear Commissioner,

We respectfully request reconsideration of the decision denying our water billing dispute based solely on the amount of time that had passed.

This request has never been about avoiding payment. It has always been about determining whether we were billed accurately during a period when the property’s original water meter was being replaced as part of the City’s meter modernization program.

When we purchased our home more than three years ago, it still had its original water meter. During the transfer of utility service into our names, the water was shut off, and we spent our very first night in our home without running water. City personnel were involved in restoring service during that process.

Not long afterward, we received an unusually high water bill. Like any reasonable homeowner, we contacted the Water Department because we believed something was wrong.

Around that same time, the City began replacing older water meters with updated technology. Our property became part of that program.

What should have been a routine meter replacement became much more involved. The water shutoff first had to be located before work could continue. We were then informed by the City technician that he was not authorized to perform the plumbing work necessary to complete the installation because the existing meter connections required repair.

As a result, we had to hire a licensed plumber, at our own expense, before the City could return and complete the meter replacement.

These circumstances resulted in multiple appointments, contractor scheduling, plumbing repairs, additional expenses, and delays that were outside of our control.

Despite these circumstances, when our request was ultimately reviewed, the focus was not whether the original bill accurately reflected our water usage. Instead, the request was denied because too much time had passed.

Respectfully, we believe that decision does not adequately consider the unique circumstances surrounding this matter.

The delays were directly connected to the City’s meter replacement process, the condition of the existing installation, and repairs that had to be completed before the replacement could occur.

A reasonable homeowner would expect that when delays arise during a City-directed infrastructure project, those circumstances would be taken into account when evaluating a billing dispute.

We understand that Toledo’s ordinances establish deadlines for filing appeals. We also understand those ordinances provide discretion when extenuating circumstances exist. We respectfully believe our situation warrants that consideration.

Accordingly, we request:

* Reconsideration of our billing dispute.

* A review of the original meter readings and billing calculations.

* A review of all work orders, technician notes, and service records associated with our property.

* Consideration of the delays caused by locating the shutoff, completing required plumbing repairs, and scheduling the City’s return to install the new meter.

* A written explanation supporting the original billing if the City concludes that no adjustment is appropriate.

Our goal is straightforward.

We simply want to know whether the original bill was accurate.

If it was accurate, we will accept that conclusion once it has been fully explained and supported by the available evidence.

If it was not, we respectfully request that our account be corrected.

We appreciate your time and respectfully request a response.

articles.title: From the Gas Fields to the Server Farm: What Ohio's Energy Boom Teaches Us About Data Centers
articles.topic: Data centers, energy, and the economy
articles.summary: Connects Ohio's natural gas boom to its rapid data center expansion: the server farms need the energy the gas fields supply. He places both in the state's longer pattern of economic shifts, from railroads and steel to highways and logistics, and examines what the new development means for jobs, power, and communities.
articles.full_text:
From the Gas Fields to the Server Farm: What Ohio’s Energy Boom Teaches Us About Data Centers

Introduction

Every generation experiences an economic shift that changes where businesses invest and where jobs are created. In the nineteenth century, railroads and steel helped shape Ohio’s industrial growth. In the twentieth century, highways, manufacturing, and logistics transformed the state again. Today, a new kind of development is reshaping parts of Ohio: the natural gas boom and the rapid expansion of data centers.

At first glance, these two trends may seem unrelated. Natural gas drilling takes place in the ground, while data centers are filled with computers, servers, and cooling systems. But they are closely connected. Data centers need enormous amounts of electricity, reliable infrastructure, and long-term energy planning. Ohio’s gas boom has helped make the state more attractive to companies that want to build and operate these facilities.

To understand what this means for Ohio’s future, it helps to look at how energy, technology, and economic development work together. The rise of natural gas production and the growth of data centers show how one industry can create opportunities for another, while also raising important questions about jobs, land use, and the environment.

Ohio’s Gas Boom

In the early twenty-first century, Ohio became part of a major natural gas and oil expansion tied to shale drilling, especially in the Utica Shale region. Advances in drilling technology made it possible to extract resources that were once difficult to reach. As production increased, Ohio gained new energy infrastructure, new investment, and new attention from businesses looking for affordable power.

The gas boom brought economic benefits to many communities. It created jobs in drilling, transportation, equipment manufacturing, construction, and support services. Landowners in some areas received lease payments and royalties. Local governments also saw new tax revenue from energy-related activity.

At the same time, the boom changed how people thought about Ohio’s energy future. Natural gas became an important part of the state’s power supply, helping utilities meet demand and support industrial growth. For companies that need large amounts of electricity, this mattered a great deal.

Why Data Centers Are Moving to Ohio

Data centers are buildings that store and process digital information. They power cloud computing, online shopping, streaming services, artificial intelligence, banking systems, and countless other parts of modern life. Because they run thousands of servers at once, they require constant electricity, strong internet connections, and advanced cooling systems.

Ohio has become attractive to data center companies for several reasons. First, the state has access to relatively affordable energy, including natural gas. Second, Ohio sits in a strong geographic location with good transportation and communication networks. Third, the state has land available for large facilities, especially near growing metropolitan areas such as Columbus, New Albany, and central Ohio suburbs.

For companies that want to build data centers, these advantages matter. A facility that runs day and night cannot afford frequent power interruptions or high energy costs. Natural gas helps support the kind of reliable electricity supply these businesses need.

How the Two Trends Connect

The connection between Ohio’s gas boom and data centers is simple but powerful: energy attracts technology, and technology increases energy demand.

Natural gas helps generate electricity that data centers depend on. In turn, data centers create new demand for power plants, transmission lines, and utility planning. This relationship means that energy development and digital infrastructure are now linked in ways that affect the entire state economy.

In some places, data centers are being built near areas with strong utility access and industrial infrastructure. In others, companies are choosing Ohio because they believe the state can support long-term growth better than regions with higher energy costs or less available land.

This pattern shows how one industry can encourage another. Just as railroads once helped factories grow, and highways once helped suburbs expand, energy resources today are helping digital infrastructure spread.

Why This Matters for Ohio

The growth of data centers can bring important benefits. Construction projects create jobs for electricians, engineers, contractors, and suppliers. Once facilities are operating, they support technical positions in maintenance, security, and operations. They also bring tax revenue and can strengthen local utility systems.

For Ohio, this means the gas boom may help support a new kind of economy. Instead of relying only on traditional manufacturing, the state can also become a center for digital infrastructure. That can make Ohio more competitive in a world where cloud computing and artificial intelligence are becoming essential.

However, the benefits are not automatic. Data centers do not employ huge numbers of workers once construction is finished. A single facility may require a large investment but only a relatively small permanent staff. That means communities must think carefully about whether the tax revenue and infrastructure improvements are worth the tradeoffs.

Challenges and Concerns

Like any major development trend, the gas boom and data center expansion raise important concerns.

One concern is environmental impact. Natural gas is cleaner than some other fossil fuels, but it still produces greenhouse gas emissions. Communities that rely heavily on gas must consider long-term climate goals and the future of energy policy.

Data centers also use large amounts of electricity and, in many cases, water for cooling. As more facilities are built, local utilities may need to expand generation and transmission capacity. That can affect rates, land use, and planning decisions for nearby residents.

Another concern is whether the economic benefits are shared fairly. Some communities may receive new tax revenue and construction work, while others see little long-term employment growth. Residents may ask whether incentives offered to attract data centers are worth the public cost.

There is also the question of resilience. If Ohio becomes too dependent on one kind of energy or one kind of digital infrastructure, it may face risks if market conditions change. Smart planning requires balancing growth with flexibility.

Similar Patterns Across Time

The relationship between Ohio’s gas boom and data centers follows a familiar historical pattern.

First, a new resource or technology creates opportunity. Then businesses move in to take advantage of lower costs and better infrastructure. Communities hope for jobs and investment. Over time, the region changes as new industries reshape the economy.

This pattern has happened many times in Ohio’s history. Coal, steel, automobiles, and manufacturing all transformed the state in different eras. Today, natural gas and digital infrastructure are doing something similar.

The lesson is that economic growth often depends on more than one industry. Energy supports technology. Technology supports business. Business supports communities. When these systems work together, they can create powerful new opportunities.

Lessons for the Future

Ohio’s experience offers several lessons for the future.

First, energy policy matters. Businesses that need reliable power will choose places where electricity is affordable and dependable. States that plan wisely can attract investment.

Second, communities should think beyond short-term gains. A new data center may bring construction jobs and tax revenue, but local leaders should also consider long-term environmental effects, infrastructure needs, and public benefits.

Third, workers need adaptable skills. As Ohio’s economy changes, people will need training in electrical work, computer systems, engineering, logistics, and energy management. Education and workforce development will be essential.

Finally, growth should be balanced with responsibility. Natural gas and data centers can help Ohio compete in the modern economy, but they should be developed in ways that protect communities and support sustainable progress.

Conclusion

Ohio’s gas boom and the rise of data centers are part of the same larger story: the way energy shapes economic development. Natural gas has helped make Ohio more attractive to companies that need reliable, affordable electricity. Data centers, in turn, are bringing new investment and helping define the state’s role in the digital economy.

Like earlier industrial changes, this transition brings both promise and challenge. It can create jobs, strengthen infrastructure, and attract business. It can also raise concerns about the environment, public costs, and long-term planning.

The future of Ohio will depend on how well leaders, businesses, and communities manage these changes. If they plan wisely, the state can benefit from both its energy resources and its growing digital economy. The lesson is clear: in the modern world, power does not just come from the ground or from the grid. It comes from how people choose to use both.

Ralph K
