articles.title: A Kingdom Response to Powerful Services
articles.summary: Addresses strong reactions to services where people cry, shout, run, shake, or fall during worship: some assume it is fake, others assume everything must be from God, and a Kingdom response rushes to neither extreme. He works from Pentecost onward and argues for discernment that tests what is happening while keeping the focus on Christ.
articles.full_text:
People often react strongly when they see a church service where the Holy Spirit moves in a powerful way. In some services, people may cry, shout, run across the room, jump, shake, fall to the floor, or even scream during prayer or worship. To someone who has never seen that before, it can look confusing or chaotic. Some people immediately assume it is fake or emotional hype. Others assume everything happening must automatically be from God. A Kingdom response does not rush to either extreme.

The Bible shows that when God moves among people, unusual reactions sometimes happen. At Pentecost, the disciples were filled with the Spirit and began speaking in other languages. The people watching did not understand what they were seeing. Some even accused them of being drunk because of the intensity of the moment. From the outside, the scene looked strange.

Another example appears when the temple was dedicated under Solomon. The presence of God filled the temple so strongly that the priests could not even remain standing to continue their work. Encounters with God sometimes overwhelm normal human composure.

Because of that, strong reactions today should not automatically be dismissed. When someone feels deep conviction, relief, repentance, or joy, the response can be emotional and physical. Some people cry. Some fall to their knees. Some shout or run because they feel a sudden release from guilt or fear. These moments can feel very real and very powerful to the person experiencing them.

Healing is also part of the biblical record. During the ministry of Jesus Christ, people who were blind received sight, people who could not walk stood up and walked, and physical conditions changed in ways that others could see. These were not vague feelings or emotional encouragement. They were tangible events.

But the Bible also gives a clear warning. Not every emotional moment, dramatic reaction, or claimed miracle is automatically the work of God. Human emotion, group energy, misunderstanding, exaggeration, and sometimes manipulation can also produce powerful scenes. Because of this, Scripture repeatedly tells believers to test what they see rather than blindly accept or instantly reject it.

The Kingdom approach is steady and disciplined.

First, look at the fruit instead of the spectacle. If a moment leads people toward repentance, humility, and a deeper commitment to Jesus Christ, that lines up with the work of the Spirit. If the focus shifts toward personalities, hype, or confusion, something is wrong.

Second, remember the main mission of the Spirit. The work of the Spirit is not centered on dramatic displays. The Spirit points people to Christ, convicts hearts of truth, and transforms character. Sometimes that happens quietly. Sometimes it happens in a powerful public moment.

Another issue appears in modern church culture. Some ministries highlight the most dramatic moments in their services. Videos of people falling, shaking, screaming, or claiming instant healing can spread quickly online. These scenes attract attention and curiosity. Over time, the experience itself can become the main attraction.

When that happens, a service can slowly shift from worship and teaching into something closer to a performance. People may begin attending not to seek truth, but to witness a powerful moment. Leaders can also feel pressure to reproduce the same atmosphere every week.

In some situations, these moments are also connected to fundraising. After a dramatic scene, a speaker may encourage people to give money, sometimes describing it as a “seed” connected to blessing, healing, or favor from God.

Scripture directly warns against treating spiritual power like a transaction. In the book of Acts, a man named Simon the Sorcerer tried to offer money to receive spiritual authority. The apostles strongly rebuked him because the things of God cannot be bought.

The ministry of Jesus shows the same principle. Jesus healed people, taught truth, and helped the poor without charging them for access to God. The Kingdom was never presented as a service people had to pay for.

This does not mean every church that receives donations is doing something wrong. Churches have always relied on voluntary giving to support ministry, help people in need, and maintain their work in the community.

The concern appears when emotional or spiritual moments are used as leverage. When people are led to believe that giving money will unlock healing, miracles, or greater spiritual favor, the line between ministry and manipulation becomes very thin.

A mature Kingdom response stays balanced. Genuine encounters with God can happen. People may experience conviction, emotional release, or even healing. Those moments can be real and deeply personal.

At the same time, believers are called to remain watchful and grounded. The focus should never be the spectacle. It should never be the personality on stage. It should never be the offering plate.

The focus remains on Christ, the one who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”

Ralph K

articles.title: The Dedication of Solomon's Temple
articles.summary: A teaching post on the dedication of Solomon's temple from 2 Chronicles 5 and 7 and 1 Kings 8: the Ark of the Covenant carried into the Most Holy Place, the musicians and sacrifices, and the presence of God made tangible to a gathered nation. He presents it as one of the clearest moments in the Bible of a large group experiencing God's presence at the same time.
articles.full_text:
The moment connected to Solomon happened when the temple in Jerusalem was completed and dedicated to God. The event is recorded in Second Chronicles chapter 5 and 7 and also in First Kings chapter 8.

For years Israel had worshiped using the Tabernacle, a portable tent system built during the time of Moses. Solomon later built a permanent temple in Jerusalem as the central place of worship for the nation. When construction was finished, the Ark of the Covenant was brought into the inner sanctuary of the temple.

The Ark represented the covenant between God and Israel. It was placed in the most sacred room, called the Most Holy Place. Priests carried the Ark inside while the people gathered outside and sacrifices were offered. Musicians and singers also worshiped with instruments and voices.

At that moment something unusual happened.

Scripture says a cloud filled the temple. The cloud represented the glory and presence of God. The Hebrew word often used for this is the “glory” or “weight” of God’s presence. The experience was not symbolic. It was described as a visible and overwhelming manifestation.

The priests who were standing in the temple suddenly could not continue their duties. The presence of God became so strong that they could not remain standing to minister. Worship stopped because the people were overwhelmed by what was happening.

The text explains the reason clearly. It says the house of the Lord was filled with the glory of God.

This event matters because it shows a physical and tangible encounter with God’s presence. It was not just emotional excitement or organized ceremony. Something happened that the people could see and feel. The atmosphere of the room changed to the point that trained priests could not continue their work.

Later in the same dedication period, Solomon prayed publicly for the nation. After his prayer, fire came down from heaven and consumed the sacrifices on the altar. Again the glory of the Lord filled the temple and the people fell facedown in worship.

This moment established the temple as the official center of worship for Israel. It also showed that God accepted the temple and the sacrifices being offered there.

Several important patterns appear in the event.

First, the experience happened during worship and dedication, not as entertainment. The people were honoring God and offering sacrifice.

Second, the focus was not on individuals having personal experiences. The entire gathering recognized that the presence of God had filled the place.

Third, the result was humility and reverence. The people bowed down and worshiped. The moment did not elevate a personality or create a show.

The account of Solomon’s temple dedication shows that encounters with God can be powerful and even physically overwhelming. At the same time, the purpose was to direct attention toward God’s holiness and authority, not toward spectacle.

It stands as one of the clearest examples in the Bible of a large group of people experiencing the tangible presence of God at the same time.

articles.title: The Attack at Temple Israel
articles.summary: His report and response on the attack that day at Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, where a man drove a vehicle into one of the largest Reform synagogues in the United States and gunfire followed, with about 140 children inside the early childhood center and none injured. He places it against rising Israel and Iran tensions and closes with counsel: stay steady, and do not surrender to fear.
articles.full_text:
A frightening situation unfolded today at Temple Israel, one of the largest Reform synagogues in the United States. Around midday, a man drove a vehicle into the building and gunfire followed. Security personnel engaged the attacker and the suspect died at the scene. About 140 children were inside the synagogue’s early childhood center at the time, but none of them were injured. One security guard was struck by the vehicle and hospitalized but is expected to recover. Authorities later found explosive materials and a rifle in the vehicle, and federal investigators are now involved.  ￼

This incident did not happen in a vacuum. The world is already on edge. The past few years have seen rising tensions between Israel and Iran, including missile and drone attacks and direct military strikes between the two nations. In 2024 and 2025, Iran launched large-scale missile and drone attacks against Israel after Israeli strikes on Iranian targets.  ￼

When conflicts grow overseas, the pressure often shows up in communities far away. Jewish institutions around the world have increased security because threats tend to rise whenever the Middle East becomes unstable. The attack in Michigan happened during a time when Jewish communities globally have been on heightened alert.  ￼

That reality can make people feel anxious or even afraid. But fear is not the correct response. Awareness is.

There is a difference between panic and preparation. Panic causes confusion. Preparation protects people. What happened at Temple Israel shows why security matters. Someone was watching. Someone was ready. When the threat appeared, security acted and prevented something much worse.

This is the kind of world we live in right now. International conflicts spill into social tensions. Ideology, hate, and political anger sometimes drive unstable people to act locally. Pretending it cannot happen does not help anyone.

The correct posture is calm awareness.

Pay attention to your surroundings. Notice exits when you enter buildings. Trust your instincts if something feels wrong. Support security teams that protect schools and houses of worship. These simple habits strengthen communities.

At the same time, we refuse to live in fear.

Acts like this try to send a message of intimidation. The goal is to scare people away from gathering, worshipping, or living normally. That goal must fail.

Places of worship exist because people believe that good is stronger than evil. Violence does not change that truth.

Today the Jewish community in Michigan experienced a moment of danger. But because of preparation and quick action, lives were protected.

Stand with them. Pray for the injured security guard. Appreciate the people who stopped the attack.

Keep your head up.
Stay aware.
Stay steady.
Do not surrender to fear.

Ralph K

articles.title: Surviving, Not Living: Faith When the Body Hurts
articles.summary: An honest piece about faith when the body hurts every single day and nothing seems to change it: life shrinks, normal things like eating and sleeping become work, and survival mode changes how a person thinks. He writes from inside that experience about still standing and returning to Jesus as the anchor.
articles.full_text:
People talk about faith like it automatically makes life peaceful. They say trust God, be thankful, stay patient. That sounds good when life is going normally. It feels very different when your body is hurting every single day and nothing you try seems to change it.

When physical problems hit and stay there for weeks or months, life starts to feel smaller. Things that should be normal—eating, relaxing, sleeping—start to feel like work. You wake up already tired. The same discomfort follows you through the day. You go to bed hoping tomorrow will be different, but then the next day starts the same way.

After a while it stops feeling like living.

It feels like surviving.

Survival mode changes how a person thinks. Instead of enjoying the day, the mind focuses on getting through the next hour. Every bite of food, every movement, every moment of rest gets interrupted by the same physical struggle. When it repeats long enough, frustration builds. You start asking why nothing is changing. You wonder why you’re supposed to be patient when every day already feels like a battle.

Trying treatments and routines without relief makes it worse. Medication doesn’t seem to help. Eating right doesn’t seem to help. People around you might try to encourage you, but it can still feel like nobody really understands what it’s like inside your body all day.

When pain lasts that long, the mind starts protecting itself. Some people begin to feel disconnected from their own body. It can feel like your brain is stepping back from the physical suffering just to cope with the mental pressure. The body is still dealing with the pain, but the mind tries to shut part of it out so it doesn’t completely break down.

That creates a strange feeling. You know something is wrong physically, but at the same time you feel detached, like your brain is trying to distance itself from what your body is experiencing. It can make everything feel unreal, heavy, and exhausting at the same time.

That kind of pressure pushes people to their limits. Sleep gets worse. Focus gets harder. Emotions get stronger. Someone who once felt normal and steady can start feeling trapped inside their own body. After months of that kind of struggle, it is not surprising when frustration and anger start showing up.

People also start directing those questions toward God.

Many assume anger toward God means someone has lost their faith. In reality, it often means the opposite. When someone is hurting deeply and still talking to God about it, they are still expecting Him to hear them. The Bible itself shows people crying out to God in confusion and frustration during long seasons of suffering.

What many people are really saying in those moments is simple: they want their life back.

Not a perfect life. Just a normal one. The ability to eat without thinking about pain. The ability to relax without their body fighting them. The ability to wake up and enjoy being alive again instead of bracing for another long day.

That is not selfish. That is human.

After enough disappointment, something eventually changes inside a person. When people, systems, or answers fail enough times, the expectations start falling away. The frustration burns through the illusions. A person reaches the point where they stop looking around for someone else to finally fix everything.

Then a decision gets made.

Enough.

Enough chasing answers in every direction. Enough letting disappointment control the story. Enough expecting people to carry something they cannot carry.

That is often when someone turns back to Christ.

Not because everything suddenly feels good. Not because the pain instantly disappears. But because they realize something important. People can fail. Systems can fail. Advice can fail.

Christ doesn’t.

And sometimes that moment takes courage.

It takes courage to admit you are exhausted. It takes courage to admit you are angry and confused. It takes courage to stop pretending everything is fine and return to the only place that never actually turned you away.

Coming back to Jesus is not weakness. It is a decision. A decision to stand on something solid when everything else feels unstable.

The storm may still be there.

But the direction has changed.

Ralph K

articles.title: The Bible Has a Real Meaning
articles.summary: Answers the claim that everyone just interprets the Bible through their background, church, or culture. Backgrounds shape reading, he grants, but if the Bible had no real meaning, communication itself would be impossible; its authors intended specific claims, and careful reading can recover what they meant.
articles.full_text:
People often say that everyone just interprets the Bible based on their background, their church, or their culture. There is some truth in that. Every person approaches a text with assumptions. We all have teachers, traditions, and experiences that shape how we read things. No one comes to any book as a completely blank slate.

But recognizing that people interpret the Bible does not mean the Bible has no real meaning. If that were true, communication would be impossible. Words would mean whatever each reader decided. Language works because authors intend to say something and readers can understand that meaning with careful reading.

The Bible was written by real people in real historical settings. They were communicating specific claims about God, humanity, sin, and redemption. Those claims can be studied. Context matters. Language matters. History matters. When people take those things seriously, the main message of the Bible becomes very clear.

Throughout history, Christians have debated certain topics. That is true. But there has also been strong agreement on the core claims of the faith. For nearly two thousand years, Christians across cultures have agreed that God is the creator, that humanity is broken by sin, that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, that He died and rose again, and that salvation comes through Him. These ideas did not appear randomly in modern churches. They were recognized very early and repeated across generations.

The Bible itself is a collection of different types of writing. Some parts are history. Some are poetry. Some are prophecy. Some are letters. Recognizing these different styles does not weaken the Bible. It actually helps people read it more carefully. Poetry should not be read like a legal document, and a historical narrative should not be treated like a metaphor. Each part should be understood according to how it was written.

Another claim people often make is that Jesus rejected the authority of Scripture. But when we actually look at the Gospels, we see the opposite. Jesus quoted the Hebrew Scriptures often. When He was challenged or tempted, He responded with “It is written.” He corrected people who misused Scripture, but He never treated it as unimportant. Instead, He pointed people back to its true meaning.

The real issue usually appears at the end of these conversations. If the Bible is not the authority, something else must take its place. Most of the time that “something” becomes the individual person. Truth becomes whatever feels right to someone in the moment.

The Bible warns about that exact problem. Human judgment is limited. People justify what they want. History shows how easily individuals and societies convince themselves that wrong actions are right.

That is why Scripture exists in the first place. It provides an external reference point outside of personal opinion. It gives people a stable record of God’s actions and teachings so truth is not constantly reinvented by every generation.

The Bible is not worshiped. It is not God. But it is the record God provided so that people would not have to guess who He is. Without that anchor, belief quickly turns into personal preference, and truth becomes whatever the loudest voice or strongest feeling declares.

When people read the Bible carefully—looking at context, history, and the full story rather than isolated verses—the central message becomes consistent and clear. Humanity is broken, God pursues restoration, and that restoration comes through Jesus Christ.

As Jesus Himself said in Gospel of John 14:6: He is the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Him.

Ralph K

articles.title: Observable Facts, Then Interpretation
articles.summary: Separates observable facts from interpretation in a circulating claim of injustice: a protester interrupted a public hearing, security removed him, he was injured in the struggle at the doorway and later claimed a broken arm, and he was charged. He argues the story's meaning is decided in the layer added after the facts, and calls for truth over narrative and justice without partiality.
articles.full_text:
A message has been circulating online that claims a shocking example of injustice. The claim points to a moment caught on camera during a public government hearing. In the video, a man interrupts the proceedings with a protest. Security moves to remove him from the room. During the struggle at the doorway, his arm becomes trapped and he is injured. The incident is recorded and spreads quickly across social media.

Those are the observable facts. A protester interrupted an official hearing. Security removed him. During the removal he was injured, and he later claimed his arm was broken. Authorities charged him with offenses connected to the disruption and resistance during the removal.

What happens next is where interpretation enters.

The viral message takes this single filmed event and builds a larger argument around it. The statement points out that the injured protester was a white male veteran and then asks readers to imagine how much worse things must be for other groups when cameras are not present. The claim moves from a documented event to a broader conclusion about hidden abuse.

That step is not evidence. It is inference.

One incident does not automatically prove a systemic pattern. It may raise questions that deserve investigation, but questions are not the same thing as proof. Social media often blurs that line. A real event becomes the emotional spark, and then assumptions expand far beyond what the original footage actually shows.

Another layer in the message is identity framing. The argument begins by addressing people based on race. Once the conversation starts there, the rest of the narrative follows that path. One group becomes the audience. Other groups are placed into victim categories. The situation quickly becomes a story about racial conflict rather than a clear examination of what actually happened in the room.

Then the message escalates further by applying extreme political language. Terms like “fascism” are invoked. Historically, fascism refers to authoritarian regimes where the state suppresses opposition and centralizes power under a controlling leader. When that word is used in modern political arguments, it often functions more as an alarm signal than a precise description of a political system. The result is emotional escalation rather than careful analysis.

The final step in the message is a call for people to “get into the fight.” At that point the goal is no longer understanding. The goal is mobilization.

This pattern appears constantly in modern media cycles. A real event happens. The event is framed through identity categories. The interpretation expands beyond the available facts. Strong ideological labels are applied. Then readers are urged to join a political battle.

A Kingdom response approaches the situation differently.

The first question is always truth. What actually happened? What evidence exists? What parts of the story are verified and what parts are speculation? Truth matters because justice cannot exist without it.

The second question is justice itself. If someone was harmed, that harm should be examined honestly. Violence and abuse are wrong regardless of who commits them or who suffers from them. Justice does not depend on race, politics, or group identity.

The third question is division. The Kingdom does not organize people into moral camps based on skin color or social categories. Scripture repeatedly warns against favoritism and partiality. Every person stands equal before God, both in dignity and in the need for redemption.

Finally, the Kingdom rejects the constant pressure to turn every event into a tribal fight. Modern media thrives on outrage because outrage spreads quickly. But outrage rarely produces clarity or reconciliation. It produces deeper camps and louder accusations.

A single event can reveal something important. It can raise legitimate concerns about conduct, authority, or justice. But responsible truth handling requires separating what is known from what is assumed. When those lines disappear, narratives take control and truth becomes secondary.

The Kingdom path remains steady: verify facts, pursue justice without partiality, refuse identity-based division, and remember that the deeper human problem is not race or politics. The deeper problem is the condition of the human heart. Christ addresses that root, which is why the Kingdom does not begin with social tribes. It begins with truth and redemption.

articles.title: All That and a Bag of Chips
articles.summary: Traces the slang phrase 'all that and a bag of chips' from late 1980s and early 1990s meal deals to its everyday use for someone who brings the full package and a little extra. He turns the phrase toward faith, abundance, and giving God the glory rather than pride.
articles.full_text:
People sometimes say the phrase “all that and a bag of chips.” It sounds like simple slang, but the meaning behind it is easy to understand. It describes someone who has the main thing covered and still brings something extra.

The phrase grew out of American slang in the late 1980s and early 1990s. A basic meal might come with a sandwich or burger. If someone added a bag of chips, it meant you got a little more than expected. The meal was already enough, but the extra made it better.

When the phrase moved into everyday speech, people started using it to describe a person who stands out. Someone who is skilled, dependable, or impressive. In that sense, saying someone is “all that and a bag of chips” can simply mean they bring the full package. They show up ready, they do the job well, and they even add something extra.

Sometimes the phrase is used sarcastically. If a person acts proud or full of themselves, people might say it to point out the attitude. But it can also be a genuine compliment when someone has clearly earned respect.

There is an interesting Kingdom connection here if you step back and look at it through the pattern of scripture.

Throughout the Bible, God’s way of providing is not just about barely getting by. Again and again the pattern is provision first, then overflow. The need is met, and then there is extra.

Jesus explains this in Matthew 6:33. He tells people to seek the Kingdom of God first and live rightly, and the things they need will be added to them. The order matters. The focus is on God and His Kingdom, and the provision follows.

Paul describes the same pattern in Ephesians 3:20. He writes that God is able to do far more than we ask or even imagine. That is the language of abundance, not scarcity.

You can see this clearly in the life of Jesus. When He feeds thousands of people with a few loaves and fish, everyone eats until they are full. Afterward, the disciples gather baskets of leftovers. The crowd receives what they need, and there is still more left over. That account appears in John 6.

The pattern is simple. God provides the meal. Sometimes there is still a “bag of chips” left afterward.

The important difference is where the credit belongs.

Human culture often turns success into personal status. A person starts believing they are the reason for their own gifts. Pride grows and the focus shifts inward.

Scripture corrects that idea. In James 1:17, it says that every good and perfect gift comes from above. Ability, opportunity, intelligence, creativity, leadership—these are not random accidents. They are gifts given by God.

That means recognizing excellence is not wrong. A person can do something well. They can work hard, grow in skill, and carry responsibility with strength. There is nothing wrong with acknowledging that.

The Kingdom difference is remembering the source.

So when someone says a person is “all that and a bag of chips,” the statement can simply mean they are bringing quality, skill, and reliability. The compliment recognizes the visible work.

The Kingdom view just keeps the bigger picture clear. The gift may be real, and the extra may be obvious, but the supply did not start with the person holding it. The supply came from God.

articles.title: The Meaning of Life Is a Person
articles.summary: Contrasts the answers cultures give to the meaning of life, happiness, knowledge, improving the world, legacy, with the Bible's approach: instead of a theory, it points to a person. Working through John 14:6, he ties the way to direction, the truth to reality, and the life to what people are actually looking for.
articles.full_text:
People have asked about the meaning of life for a long time. Philosophers, religions, and whole cultures have tried to answer it. Some say life is about being happy. Others say it is about gaining knowledge, improving the world, or leaving something behind after you die.

The Bible approaches the question in a different way. Instead of giving a theory, it points to a person.

In Gospel of John 14:6, Jesus Christ says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” This is a clear statement. He is not just offering advice or a philosophy. He is saying that the meaning of life is connected directly to Him.

Each part of that statement connects to a question people naturally ask.

First is the way.

People want direction. At some point almost everyone wonders where their life is supposed to go. Many things try to offer guidance—politics, culture, self-help ideas, or religious systems. But those directions often change depending on trends, leaders, or public opinion.

Jesus makes a different claim. He does not hand out a list of steps or a program to follow. He says He Himself is the way. That means the path of life is not just about rules or strategies. It is about following Him and aligning your life with Him.

Second is the truth.

People also want to know what is real. Truth answers questions about how the world actually works and what is trustworthy. In modern culture, truth is often treated as something personal, something each person can define for themselves.

Jesus makes a stronger claim. He does not only say that He teaches truth. He says He is the truth. That means reality itself is anchored in Him. Truth is not decided by popularity or cultural shifts. It is rooted in who Christ is.

Third is the life.

When people ask about the meaning of life, they are really asking what their existence is for. Many chase success, money, pleasure, or recognition because they hope those things will make life feel meaningful.

But those things do not last. Success fades. Wealth changes hands. Human praise disappears over time.

Jesus connects life to something deeper. Real life is not just breathing and existing. It is being restored into relationship with God and living as part of His Kingdom. The Bible describes this as eternal life, and it begins now, not only after death.

When these three parts come together, the picture becomes clearer.

The way answers direction.
The truth answers reality.
The life answers purpose.

In Christ, all three meet at the same point.

The message of the gospel is that the meaning of life is not something people build on their own through effort or achievement. It is something revealed through relationship with Jesus. Life makes sense when the path, the truth about reality, and the purpose of existence all lead back to the same source.

According to the claim in Gospel of John 14:6, the meaning of life is not just a problem to solve.

It is a person to follow.

Ralph K

articles.title: Activity Without Alignment Is Lawlessness
articles.summary: Takes Matthew 7:21-23 seriously: some will prophesy, cast out demons, and do powerful works in Jesus' name and still hear 'I never knew you,' because the dividing line is doing the Father's will. He connects it to James 2:17 and concludes that faith without works is dead, activity without alignment is lawlessness, and the Kingdom runs on obedience, not noise.
articles.full_text:
The warning in Gospel of Matthew 7:21–23 is direct. Jesus Christ says not everyone who calls Him “Lord” will enter the Kingdom. Some will prophesy in His name. Some will cast out demons. Some will do powerful works. And He will still say, “I never knew you. Depart from me.”

That statement should slow us down.

The issue is not whether they believed He existed. The issue is not whether they were active in ministry. The issue is obedience. “He who does the will of My Father.” That is the dividing line.

Now connect that to Epistle of James 2:17: “Faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.” James is not arguing for earning salvation. He is exposing a faith that talks but does not submit. Dead faith agrees with truth but refuses transformation. It uses spiritual language but resists surrender.

Matthew exposes performance without relationship. James exposes belief without obedience. They are saying the same thing from different angles.

This is where Martin Luther comes in. During the Protestant Reformation, Luther rightly confronted corruption and restored the doctrine that justification is by faith, not by works of the law. That correction was necessary. The Church had drifted into merit systems and indulgences.

But in reacting against legalism, Luther struggled with James. He famously called it an “epistle of straw.” He emphasized “faith alone,” guarding grace. The problem was not his defense of grace. The problem was the long-term imbalance that developed in some Protestant streams. “Faith alone” became, in practice, “belief alone.” Obedience was treated as optional or secondary.

Scripture does not teach salvation by works. It also does not teach salvation without transformation.

Paul fights legalism — the idea that works produce salvation.
James fights dead belief — the idea that salvation produces no change.

Both are needed. Remove either one and distortion enters.

Look at contemporary patterns.

We have seen celebrity ministers preach powerfully, build large platforms, then fall through abuse, manipulation, or hidden sin. The name of Jesus was used. The fruit of obedience was missing. That is Matthew 7 in modern clothing.

We see prosperity-focused ministries associated with figures like Kenneth Copeland or Joel Osteen. Not identical in theology, but similar in emphasis. Blessing, increase, favor. Less emphasis on repentance, suffering, or cross-bearing. Faith becomes a tool for outcomes rather than surrender to the will of God. The issue is not wealth itself. The issue is transactional faith.

We see hyper-grace movements influenced by teachers such as Joseph Prince. Strong teaching on the finished work of Christ. In some interpretations, weak emphasis on ongoing obedience. When grace is detached from transformation, people can feel spiritually secure while remaining unchanged.

We also see political Christianity across parties. Public identification with Christ while defending dishonesty, cruelty, or power at any cost. The banner says “Lord.” The behavior reflects another allegiance.

Dead faith today is not quiet. It is active. It builds stages, raises money, runs media campaigns, fills conferences, and posts verses. It looks alive. But if obedience to the Father’s will is absent, it is spiritually dead.

So what is the Kingdom response?

First, repentance. Not PR adjustments. Not brand repair. Real turning. Where confession has outrun obedience, alignment must be restored.

Second, fruit inspection without hysteria. The Kingdom does not measure success by numbers, influence, or revenue. It measures conformity to Christ’s character — truthfulness, humility, mercy, purity, self-control.

Third, remove personality worship. When leaders become brands, accountability dies. Kingdom structure requires shared authority and real correction.

Fourth, re-center the cross. The cross is not decoration. It is the pattern. It kills pride, greed, domination, and manipulation. Any stream that bypasses the cross will drift into lawlessness.

Fifth, accept obscurity. Living faith often looks small and ordinary. It obeys when unseen. It repents quickly. It values integrity over platform.

The collapse of dead faith is not the fall of Christ’s Church. It is pruning.

Matthew 7 is not written to scare unbelievers. It is written to warn those who use His name. James 2 is not attacking grace. It is defending living faith.

The line is clear:
Confession without obedience is empty.
Belief without surrender is dead.
Activity without alignment is lawlessness.

The Kingdom does not run on noise. It runs on obedience.

articles.title: The Thorn in My Side
articles.summary: Works through Paul's thorn in the flesh in 2 Corinthians 12:7-10: given to keep him from pride, asked away three times, and answered with 'My grace is sufficient for you.' He notes Paul never names the thorn, so Scripture explains the purpose rather than the diagnosis, and suggests the thing a person begs God to remove may be what keeps them grounded, steady, and aligned.
articles.full_text:
The Thorn in My Side

Paul talks about his “thorn in the flesh” in Second Epistle to the Corinthians 12:7–10. He says it was given to keep him from becoming proud after receiving powerful revelation. He asked the Lord three times to take it away. The answer was no. Instead he heard, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is made perfect in weakness.”

Paul never names the thorn. That silence is important. Scripture explains the purpose, not the diagnosis.

Some believe it was a physical illness. In Epistle to the Galatians 4:13–15 Paul mentions preaching while sick, and some think it involved his eyes. Others believe it was constant persecution, since his life in Acts of the Apostles shows repeated beatings, prison, and public opposition. He also calls it a “messenger of Satan,” which points to ongoing spiritual pressure.

What we know for certain:

It was persistent.
It made him weak.
It followed deep revelation.
It was not removed.
It became the place where Christ’s power showed up.

That is the pattern. Revelation leads to elevation. Elevation creates the risk of pride. Pride invites collapse. So pressure is permitted to guard the heart.

We live in a culture of constant exposure. Influence can grow quickly. Insight can gain attention. A strong moment can turn into a platform overnight. The system rewards projection of strength. It teaches people to hide weakness and amplify image.

The Kingdom does not operate that way. It runs on dependence, not display.

The thorn exposes what a person leans on. Applause. Recognition. Control. Being right. Being seen as strong. If the pressure disappeared, would self-reliance grow? That is the issue.

Not every resistance is an attack. Not every closed door is warfare. Some pressures function as restraints. They slow pride. They keep the center anchored. They protect calling from corruption.

Paul says the thorn was a “messenger of Satan,” yet it was “given.” The adversary strikes. God limits. Permission does not equal endorsement. It reveals sovereignty. The attack humbles. The boundary preserves.

The answer Paul received was not removal. It was grace. Grace did not eliminate weakness. It empowered him inside it.

Now bring that into everyday life.

The thorn may look like chronic health issues that never fully resolve. It may be a difficult coworker who constantly challenges patience. It may be financial pressure that forces daily trust. It may be a family tension that refuses to disappear. It may be slow growth when others seem to accelerate. It may be the frustration of not being recognized for what you know you carry.

These are not glamorous struggles. They are ordinary. Repetitive. Sometimes exhausting.

But inside those spaces, character forms. Ego gets trimmed. Prayer becomes real instead of performative. Gratitude becomes intentional. Dependence becomes daily instead of theoretical.

The thorn in your side is not always proof something is wrong. It may be proof something is being shaped. It may be the guardrail preventing drift. It may be the quiet mechanism keeping your heart from hardening or inflating.

Weakness does not disqualify usefulness. In Paul’s case, it was the condition that made the power of Christ visible.

In everyday life, the same principle stands. The pressure you wish would disappear may be the very thing keeping you grounded, steady, and aligned.

articles.title: Strange Events in the Bible Are Not Random Oddities
articles.summary: Argues that the Bible's strange events, Balaam's talking donkey, the witch of Endor, the floating axe head, the writing on the wall, are not random oddities but exposures of patterns still operating today. His example: the shock of Numbers 22 is not the talking animal but a spiritual leader who cannot perceive what is directly in front of him, and how dangerous authority without discernment becomes.
articles.full_text:
The Bible includes events that feel strange on the surface. They interrupt normal expectations. They challenge assumptions about power, control, and reality. When read carefully, these accounts are not random oddities. They expose patterns that still operate today.

In the Book of Numbers 22, Balaam is a recognized prophet traveling for financial gain. An angel blocks his path, but he cannot see it. His donkey does. The animal stops repeatedly to avoid danger. Balaam beats it in frustration. Then God allows the donkey to speak and confront him. The shock of the story is not mainly the talking animal. It is the exposure of a spiritual leader who cannot perceive what is directly in front of him. Authority without discernment becomes dangerous. Position does not guarantee clarity.

In First Book of Samuel 28, King Saul seeks guidance from a medium after he himself outlawed such practices. He is desperate because he no longer hears from God. The prophet Samuel appears and confirms Saul’s coming defeat. The event is unsettling, but the core issue is moral collapse. A ruler who once had direction now operates in fear and contradiction. When leadership abandons obedience, it eventually turns to what it once condemned.

The prophet Ezekiel, in Book of Ezekiel 4–5, performs extreme public acts. He lies on his side for extended periods. He cooks food over dung. He shaves his head and divides the hair to symbolize judgment. These actions were not theatrical for entertainment. They were physical messages aimed at a nation that ignored verbal warnings. When quiet correction fails, exposure becomes visible and uncomfortable. Persistent rebellion invites visible consequences.

In Second Book of Kings 6, a borrowed iron axe head falls into water. Elisha throws a stick into the river, and the iron floats. The event is small compared to larger miracles, but it shows something important. God’s involvement is not limited to national crises. Personal loss and ordinary problems are not beneath His attention. The scale of the problem does not determine His ability to intervene.

In Book of Daniel 5, a disembodied hand writes words of judgment on a palace wall during a royal feast. The king’s authority appears secure. The message declares it finished. That very night the kingdom falls. The supernatural element highlights a deeper reality: power structures can appear stable while already weighed and measured. External strength does not protect against internal corruption.

In Gospel of Matthew 17, Jesus is transfigured before His disciples. His appearance changes, and His divine authority is revealed briefly. Moses and Elijah appear with Him. The disciples fall in fear. The moment confirms identity. It removes ambiguity. It shows that beneath the ordinary exterior stands ultimate authority.

In Acts of the Apostles 5, people place the sick in the streets hoping Peter’s shadow might fall on them. The text records that healing occurred. The emphasis is not on superstition. It demonstrates the expansion of Christ’s authority through His followers. Alignment produces impact.

Another unsettling moment appears in Second Book of Kings 2, where youths mock the prophet Elisha and are mauled by bears after he pronounces a curse. The scene is severe. It reflects a broader rejection of prophetic authority in a culture already resisting correction. Contempt for truth carries weight. Dismissal is not neutral.

Taken together, these accounts reveal consistent themes. Pride is confronted. Blindness is exposed. Corrupt power is interrupted. Faithfulness is preserved. The strange elements draw attention, but the structure underneath remains steady. God governs history. Human authority is conditional. Actions carry consequence.

The unusual stories are not distractions. They are warnings and confirmations. They show that visible reality is not the only layer operating. They also show that accountability does not disappear simply because it is ignored.

articles.title: The Afternoon After
articles.summary: A story in second person about a woman who went to a service only because her best friend invited her, heard a message that crossed into places she never talks about, and committed her life to Christ. The piece stays with what comes next: the room gone, the music faded, the phones buzzing, and the beginning of exploring a Kingdom that was there all along.
articles.full_text:
Maybe before she went, she didn’t think much about God at all.

Maybe faith was background noise from childhood. Maybe it was something she respected but kept at a distance. Maybe she had reasons. Disappointment. Questions. Life experience. Or maybe she was just busy holding her world together.

She went because her best friend invited her. Not because she was searching. Just relationship.

Something happened in that room.

The message moved from general to precise. It crossed into places she does not talk about. It described internal battles she manages quietly. She responded. She committed her life to Christ. It felt real. Clear. Weighty.

Now it’s afternoon.

The room is gone. The music has faded. The world is still the world.

Phones buzz. News scrolls. Bills wait. Conversations continue like nothing eternal happened this morning. The air outside the church building does not glow. It hums with distraction.

A new thought moves in:

What if that was just a moment?
What if real life swallows this by Tuesday?
What if I needed hope so badly that I turned a normal service into something bigger than it was?

Life is not simple.

Old habits do not disappear quietly. Old coping systems do not resign politely. Stress will return. Pressure will return. The same relationships. The same responsibilities. The same internal patterns.

And here is the unfamiliar part:

If this was real, she will not escape life.
She will face life differently.

That difference may feel strange at first.

Before today, she may have handled stress with control.
Now she may pause before reacting.

Before today, she may have buried fear.
Now she may bring it into prayer.

Before today, she may have managed shame privately.
Now she may confront it instead of hiding it.

Unfamiliar does not mean fake.
It means alignment is replacing instinct.

The world is not built to protect sacred moments. It is built to dilute them. Attention is currency. Distraction is constant. Everything competes for emotional dominance.

The noise will try to reinterpret what happened.

“It was atmosphere.”
“It was music.”
“You were just emotional.”
“Life is more complicated than that.”

Life is complicated.

But fantasy escapes reality.
Truth changes how you walk through it.

If what happened was fantasy, she will need to recreate the feeling to keep it alive.
If what happened was Christ, it will show up in small decisions. In restraint. In patience. In clarity. In courage that does not need to announce itself.

Maybe she hasn’t just had a moment.

Maybe she has opened a door.

Maybe she has stepped into a Kingdom she has never explored before. Not a building. Not a brand. A different order. A different authority. A different center of gravity.

Kingdom does not remove real life.
It reframes it.

In this Kingdom, worth is not earned.
Peace is not manufactured.
Identity is not negotiated by performance.

Tomorrow may feel ordinary. That does not cancel today. Roots grow in silence. Formation rarely feels dramatic.

The world will try to make this small.
Distraction will try to blur it.
Routine will try to absorb it.

But if she was truly seen by God, that memory will not behave like hype. It will act like a reference point.

When anxiety rises, she will remember the peace.

When pressure builds, she will remember being known without rejection.

When confusion returns, she will remember the clarity.

Fantasy fades under pressure.
Truth stabilizes under pressure.

Maybe before she went, she did not expect to shift direction.

Now she is not escaping life.

She is walking back into it from a different center.

And alignment often feels unfamiliar before it feels natural.

Not because life got easier.

But because she may have just stepped into a Kingdom that was there all along——-
and she is only beginning to explore it.

Ralph K

articles.title: Peace and Safety: Scripture in Context
articles.summary: Responds to social media readings of 1 Thessalonians 5:3 ('Peace and safety, then sudden destruction') in light of events around Iran. He puts the verse back in its context about the Day of the Lord and spiritual complacency, and concludes believers are told to stay spiritually awake regardless of the news cycle, in every era including this one.
articles.full_text:
There’s talk on the social streams right now.

With everything unfolding around Iran, and reports about major terror figures possibly being removed, some voices are pointing to 1 Thessalonians 5:3. The verse says:

“While people are saying, ‘Peace and safety,’ destruction will come on them suddenly… and they will not escape.”

That line was written by Paul the Apostle to early Christians. It sits inside a section about the “Day of the Lord,” a biblical phrase tied to divine judgment. In context, Paul is warning believers not to drift into spiritual complacency. He contrasts people who feel secure and unprepared with those who stay alert and sober.

On social media, some interpret “peace and safety” as a sign that a global reset or false stability is forming right now. The idea is that when leaders claim order has been restored, sudden judgment follows.

That is one interpretive view. But the text itself does not name nations, modern conflicts, or specific political leaders. It describes a condition of human confidence. It warns against assuming history is under control.

Historically, many generations have applied this verse to their own moment—during the Roman Empire, both world wars, the Cold War, and after 9/11. Each time, people believed they were watching the final stage unfold. None of those events concluded the biblical timeline.

The passage functions as a moral warning, not a headline decoder.

Scripture elsewhere also cautions against celebrating destruction. Proverbs 24:17 warns against rejoicing when an enemy falls. Romans 12:19–21 places vengeance in God’s hands. The Bible consistently calls for sobriety rather than triumphalism.

There is a difference between recognizing geopolitical shifts and declaring prophetic fulfillment. The first is analysis. The second requires textual proof.

The steady reading of 1 Thessalonians 5 is this:
Human systems promise security. Stability can be sudden and fragile. Believers are told to stay spiritually awake regardless of the news cycle.

That remains true in every era, including this one.

articles.title: Narrative Substitution: 'You Are Divine'
articles.summary: A structured rebuttal of a circulating post, set out as 'The post claims / Scripture states': you are divine, the Kingdom is inside you, embody Christ consciousness. He argues the subtle exchange moves authority from Christ to the individual and makes the cross symbolic instead of substitutionary, which is why discernment matters.
articles.full_text:
The post claims:
“You are divine.”
Scripture states:
You are made in God’s image, fallen, redeemable, and dependent.

The post claims:
“The Kingdom is inside you.”
Scripture shows:
The King brings the Kingdom. The Kingdom is inseparable from the King.

The post claims:
“Embod y Christ consciousness.”
Scripture teaches:
Repent. Believe. Be born again. Follow Him.

Notice the subtle exchange:
Authority moves from Christ to the individual.
Redemption becomes self-activation.
The cross becomes symbolic instead of substitutionary.

This is why discernment matters. Not to attack people. But to recognize narrative substitution.

Social media amplifies emotionally empowering messages. “You are divine” spreads faster than “Deny yourself and follow Me.”

The difference is not small. It is foundational.

articles.title: How Do We Function in Humanity Without Losing Ourselves?
articles.summary: A personal essay about the realization that came to him last year, after decades of living and working: the core human question is how we function in humanity without losing ourselves, and his answer settled on the way, the truth, and the life. He turns it toward teenagers navigating an unstable, loud, unforgiving world, closing with 1 Timothy 4:12's call to set an example in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity.
articles.full_text:
Last year, after decades of living, working, building, searching, succeeding in some ways and failing in others, something finally clicked for me. It was not a childhood revelation or an early spiritual awakening. It came later than I expected. After a lifetime of trying to figure life out piece by piece, I realized that the core human question is simple but powerful: How do we function in humanity without losing ourselves? For me, the answer became clear in a way that felt steady and grounded — the way, the truth, and the life.

That realization changed how I see teenagers, especially those in the middle of a reality they never asked to be born into.

Many teens today are navigating a world that feels unstable, loud, and often unforgiving. They did not design the cultural climate. They did not choose the digital pressure. They did not create the social comparison loop they are now expected to survive. Yet they are asked to grow up inside it. Some are carrying anxiety, family strain, identity confusion, or silent loneliness. Some are simply tired.

That is why their courage stands out.

In a world that constantly shifts its definitions of truth, identity, and purpose, teenagers are often told to keep everything flexible. Truth is described as personal. Identity is described as fluid. Purpose is described as self-invented and endlessly adjustable. On the surface, that sounds freeing. In practice, it can feel unstable.

When everything moves, nothing holds.

Teens today face constant noise. Opinions cycle daily. Cultural standards change quickly. Success is measured publicly and instantly. The pressure to perform, to present, and to fit in is continuous. For those already having a rough time, that pressure can feel heavier.

So when a teenager in the middle of that storm chooses something steady — that is not small. That is courage.

Watching teens step forward, whether literally walking toward an altar or simply making a quiet internal decision, is deeply encouraging. It is not about hype or emotional momentum. It is about clarity under pressure. It is about a young person saying, “I need something solid.”

Choosing the way, the truth, and the life in the middle of personal struggle is especially powerful. It is one thing to choose direction when everything feels easy. It is another to choose it when you are confused, hurting, or unsure. That kind of choice reflects strength.

For someone older, like me, arriving at this clarity required humility after years of partial understanding. For a teenager in the middle of hardship, it requires trust and bravery. It may mean stepping forward while still carrying questions. It may mean choosing integrity when emotions are overwhelming. It may mean anchoring to truth even when circumstances feel unstable.

That is not weakness. It is resilience.

Teenagers who choose a steady foundation early are not avoiding reality. They are preparing to face it. With a center, they can move through difficulty without being defined by it. They can endure rough seasons without losing themselves. They can grow through adversity instead of being shaped only by it.

The world often defines freedom as doing whatever feels right in the moment. But real freedom has structure. It comes from knowing who you are and what you stand on, especially when life is not smooth. When a teenager finds that footing in the middle of struggle, it changes their trajectory.

If it took me decades to understand what anchors a human life, and a teenager in the middle of a hard season understands it now, that is not naïve. That is brave. It shows that clarity is not reserved for those who have everything figured out. It is available even in the middle of difficulty.

In a world that shifts constantly, choosing something unchanging is bold. Choosing it while having a rough time is even bolder. And when teenagers make that choice, it is not only encouraging. It is courageous.

1 Timothy 4:12 (NIV)

“Don’t let anyone look down on you because you are young, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith and in purity.”

Ralph K

articles.title: The Chemical Imbalance Story
articles.summary: Examines the serotonin theory of depression after the Moncrieff-led review found no solid evidence of a measurable serotonin deficiency in people with depression, and the professional response that the chemical imbalance was never meant as a literal, proven cause. He argues depression is complex, the biology is more complicated than early explanations suggested, and clear communication matters more than protecting old narratives.
articles.full_text:
A few years ago, a paper led by Joanna Moncrieff challenged the long-standing claim that depression is caused by a serotonin “chemical imbalance.” The review concluded that there is no solid evidence proving people with depression have a measurable serotonin deficiency. That finding did not come from a fringe source. It was published in a major psychiatric journal and reviewed existing research.

What followed created confusion. Professional groups, including the Royal College of Psychiatrists, responded by saying the serotonin imbalance theory was never meant to be taken as a literal, proven cause. They emphasized that depression is complex. It involves biology, trauma, stress, environment, genetics, and personal history. That has been written in academic literature for years.

But here is the tension. For decades, many patients were told something much simpler. They were told their depression was caused by a chemical imbalance and that medication corrected it. That message appeared in brochures, advertisements, websites, and conversations in exam rooms. It became the common explanation. Millions of people understood their suffering through that lens.

When the review came out and institutions shifted toward more nuanced language, many patients felt disoriented. They remembered exactly what they had been told. Hearing professionals now say “we never claimed that” felt like a denial of lived experience. That reaction is understandable. Trust depends on clarity.

The evidence today supports several points. First, there is no laboratory test that confirms a serotonin deficiency as the cause of depression. Second, antidepressants such as SSRIs do affect serotonin signaling in the brain. Third, clinical trials show these medications help some people, though the average benefit is moderate. The exact mechanism of improvement is still debated.

Depression is not one single disease with one single cause. It is a category that includes many different biological and psychological patterns. That makes simple explanations attractive but risky. When science is reduced to a slogan, the slogan eventually collapses.

Psychiatry is still a scientific field. It uses clinical trials, data analysis, and biological research. But science evolves. The problem was not that research changed. The problem was that public messaging became more certain than the evidence justified.

If communication had been more honest from the beginning, this backlash would not have been as strong. People can handle complexity. What they struggle with is feeling misled.

The takeaway is direct. The serotonin imbalance model is not proven as the cause of depression. Antidepressants can help some people. The biology is more complicated than early explanations suggested. Clear communication matters more than protecting old narratives.

articles.title: It Feels Like a Mess Because It Is a Mess: Immigration
articles.summary: Argues American immigration has turned into noise instead of policy, with both sides weaponizing the worst example they can find while the layered system underneath, federal law, border agencies, immigration courts, states, cities, prosecutors, keeps grinding and failing in slow motion. The confusion, he writes, is what happens when a complex system runs for decades without durable agreement or structural reform.
articles.full_text:
It feels like a mess because it is a mess.

Immigration in America has turned into noise instead of policy. Every week there is a new headline. A crime story. A protest. A border surge. A court ruling. A viral clip. Both sides grab the worst example they can find and use it like a weapon. Meanwhile the system underneath keeps grinding and failing in slow motion.

Here’s the hard truth: the problem is layered and nobody wants to deal with all the layers at once.

The federal government sets immigration law. Border agencies enforce it. Immigration courts decide cases. States run their own law enforcement systems. Cities decide whether to cooperate with federal detainers. Prosecutors choose what to charge and what to drop. Each layer has different priorities. When those priorities clash, gaps open up.

That’s where the anger comes from.

When someone with a criminal record enters the country and later commits a crime here, people see it as a total breakdown of order. They don’t care about jurisdictional nuance. They see failure. And honestly, when serious offenders slip through, that is a failure somewhere in the chain.

On the other side, you have real humanitarian pressure. Asylum claims. Economic collapse in other countries. Cartels exploiting migration routes. Families moving north because they believe it’s their only shot. That pressure doesn’t disappear just because the law says no.

Both realities exist at the same time.

The political class responds with slogans instead of structure. “Open borders.” “Close the border.” “Abolish ICE.” “Mass deportation.” Those phrases fire up voters but they don’t fix court backlogs, asylum fraud, visa overstays, cartel smuggling networks, or labor demand that pulls people across in the first place.

Then elections happen.

People worry that undocumented immigrants are voting. Under federal law, non-citizens cannot vote in federal elections. Verified cases exist, but widespread illegal voting has not been proven at scale in audits. That fear, though, connects to a deeper concern: sovereignty. People want to know that citizenship still means something and that law still means something.

When systems look weak, trust drops.

What we are watching isn’t just an immigration problem. It’s a governance credibility problem. When laws are passed but not consistently enforced, when agencies fight each other, when rhetoric is louder than results, confidence erodes.

That’s why it feels like a breakdown.

It’s not total collapse. Planes still fly. Elections still happen. Border agents still work. Courts still process cases. But it is strained, fragmented, and politically weaponized.

And regular people are left staring at the screen thinking: how is this still not fixed?

That frustration isn’t crazy. It’s what happens when a complex system runs for decades without durable agreement or structural reform.
